The forensic analyst
The threat intelligence analyst
The system owner
questions.explanation: The incident commander coordinates the response, keeps communication flowing across teams and updates management. Technical analysts provide findings.

questions.question: During an incident, who acquires and preserves digital evidence for deeper analysis and possible legal use?
options: The incident commander
The forensic analyst
The public relations team
The chief operating officer
questions.explanation: The forensic analyst performs deeper investigation and acquires and preserves digital evidence for analysis and possible legal use.

questions.question: Which role advises on notification duties and evidence handling during an incident?
options: Public relations
The security analyst
Legal counsel
The system owner
questions.explanation: Legal counsel advises on legal obligations, evidence handling, notifications and other legal considerations during response.

questions.question: What is a tabletop exercise?
options: A live attack on production systems by an outside red team
A test of every backup by restoring it to a spare server
A review of the office’s physical security and door locks
A discussion-based run-through of an incident to test plans and decisions
questions.hint: Talking it through, no real impact.
questions.explanation: A tabletop exercise is a discussion-based simulation that tests plans, responsibilities, communication and decision-making without real operational impact.

questions.question: What is the difference between an incident’s criticality and its impact?
options: Criticality is how quickly to respond; impact is how badly business is affected
Impact is how quickly to respond; criticality is how badly business is affected
Criticality only applies to servers; impact only applies to users
They are the same measure with two different names
questions.explanation: Criticality indicates how quickly a response is needed. Impact indicates how long or how severely business operations are affected.

questions.question: Disabling a compromised account and isolating the device straight away is an example of what?
options: Long-term containment
Short-term containment
Eradication
Recovery
questions.explanation: Short-term containment rapidly stops further harm, like disabling an account or isolating a host. It limits damage but doesn’t remove the root cause.

questions.question: Segmentation changes and permission reviews while full remediation is prepared are examples of what?
options: Short-term containment
Preparation
Long-term containment
Detection
questions.explanation: Long-term containment applies sustainable controls, like segmentation, patching or permission reviews, while eradication and recovery are prepared.

questions.question: What is a CMDB?
options: A firewall that inspects traffic at the application layer
A list of known attackers and their techniques
A backup of every user’s mailbox
A central database tracking systems, owners and their purpose
questions.explanation: A CMDB is a central repository that tracks systems and related information so IT and security teams understand ownership, purpose and status.

questions.question: What is the difference between an asset inventory and a risk assessment?
options: Inventory says what exists and who owns it; risk assessment says what matters most
Risk assessment lists the devices; inventory decides which ones matter most
Inventory is only for hardware; risk assessment is only for software
They are the same exercise carried out by different teams
questions.hint: What you have versus what matters.
questions.explanation: An asset inventory tells you what exists and who owns it. A risk assessment helps decide what matters most and where to prioritise resources.

questions.question: Buying cyber insurance to cover the cost of a breach is which type of risk treatment?
options: Risk acceptance
Risk transfer
Risk avoidance
Risk mitigation
questions.explanation: Risk transfer moves some financial or operational risk to another party, such as through insurance or contracts.

questions.question: Taking a high-risk legacy service offline completely is which type of risk treatment?
options: Risk transfer
Risk acceptance
Risk avoidance
Risk mitigation
questions.explanation: Risk avoidance removes the risky activity or exposure entirely. Mitigation reduces it with controls; acceptance tolerates it; transfer shifts it.

questions.question: Management formally decides a low-impact risk isn’t worth spending money to fix. What is this?
options: Risk avoidance
Risk transfer
Risk mitigation
Risk acceptance
questions.explanation: Risk acceptance is a formal decision to tolerate a risk when the impact is low or further controls aren’t cost-effective.

questions.question: What is a DMZ?
options: A separate subnet for internet-facing services, keeping them apart from the internal LAN
A part of the network where all security controls are switched off
The internal network that holds the most trusted systems
A VPN tunnel used by home workers to reach the office
questions.explanation: A DMZ (demilitarised zone) separates internet-facing services from the internal LAN, reducing direct exposure of internal systems.

questions.question: What is the difference between a single-firewall and a dual-firewall DMZ?
options: Single uses two firewalls side by side; dual uses one firewall with two cables
Single uses one firewall with several interfaces; dual puts firewalls either side of the DMZ
Single protects email only; dual protects websites only
Dual is just a single firewall with a backup power supply
questions.explanation: A single-firewall (three-legged) DMZ uses one firewall with external, internal and DMZ interfaces. A dual-firewall DMZ has separate frontend and backend firewalls.

questions.question: What does defence in depth mean?
options: Putting all security spending into one very strong firewall
Hiding servers deep inside the building
Using multiple layers of controls so one failure doesn’t expose everything
Only defending the most important server
questions.explanation: Defence in depth uses several layers of controls, so if one fails, critical systems still aren’t directly exposed.

questions.question: What does network segmentation help limit during an attack?
options: How many emails staff can send each day
How fast the internet connection can run
How many people can use Wi-Fi at once
How far an attacker can move between parts of the network
questions.explanation: Segmentation separates systems or zones to restrict access and limit attacker movement around the environment.

questions.question: What is the difference between a HIDS and a HIPS?
options: A HIDS detects and alerts; a HIPS can also act, like blocking a connection
A HIPS detects and alerts; a HIDS can also act, like removing a file
A HIDS protects networks; a HIPS protects only email servers
They are identical products sold by different vendors
questions.explanation: A host intrusion detection system detects and alerts. A host intrusion prevention system can also take defensive action automatically.

questions.question: Why might signature-based antivirus miss a brand-new piece of malware?
options: It only scans files that are over a certain size
It matches known patterns, so unseen malware has no signature yet
It only works when the device is offline
It deletes its own signature list every day
questions.hint: It needs to have seen it before.
questions.explanation: Signature-based detection matches files against known malicious signatures. It’s effective for known threats but may miss malware nobody has seen yet.

questions.question: How does EDR differ from traditional antivirus?
options: EDR only removes viruses, while antivirus investigates incidents
EDR runs on firewalls, while antivirus runs on laptops
EDR adds detailed telemetry, investigation and response, not just malware removal
EDR is an older technology that antivirus replaced
questions.explanation: AV mainly detects and removes malware. EDR provides richer endpoint telemetry, alerting, investigation and response, such as isolating a host.

questions.question: What does NGAV add to traditional antivirus?
options: A larger signature list that is updated every week
The ability to scan only email attachments
A firewall built into the antivirus program
Behavioural or predictive analysis to catch new and fileless threats
questions.explanation: Next-generation antivirus goes beyond signatures and heuristics, using behavioural or predictive techniques to identify newer or fileless threats.

questions.question: What is a Group Policy Object (GPO) used for?
options: Applying standard Windows settings to users and computers across a domain
Encrypting every file stored on a Windows server
Scanning domain computers for malware every night
Recording network traffic between domain controllers
questions.explanation: A GPO is a collection of Windows settings applied to sites, domains or OUs to standardise and secure users and computers, such as password policies.

questions.question: In what order is Group Policy processed?
options: OU, domain, site, then local
Local, site, domain, then OU
Domain, local, OU, then site
Site, OU, local, then domain
questions.explanation: Group Policy is processed Local, Site, Domain, then OU, so settings applied later, at the OU level, can override earlier ones.

questions.question: What is the difference between a NIDS and a NIPS?
options: A NIPS monitors and alerts; a NIDS sits inline and can block traffic
A NIDS protects laptops; a NIPS protects web servers only
A NIDS monitors and alerts; a NIPS sits inline and can block traffic
They are the same thing with different names
questions.explanation: A NIDS monitors traffic and alerts analysts. A NIPS sits inline in the traffic path and can automatically block or reset suspicious connections.

questions.question: What is the risk of deploying a security device inline?
options: It can only see a copy of the traffic, not the real thing
It can’t take any action to block traffic
It stops all logs from reaching the SIEM
If it fails, it can disrupt the traffic flowing through it
questions.explanation: Inline placement enables prevention, but because traffic flows through the device, a failure can create an availability problem.

questions.question: What is the difference between a network tap and a SPAN port?
options: A tap is a dedicated physical device; a SPAN port mirrors traffic on a switch
A SPAN port is a physical device; a tap is a setting on a switch
A tap blocks traffic; a SPAN port only logs it
Neither provides a copy of traffic for monitoring
questions.hint: Both copy traffic to a sensor.
questions.explanation: Both feed traffic copies to monitoring tools. A tap is a dedicated physical method; a SPAN port is a switch port configured to mirror traffic.

questions.question: Which open-source network monitoring platform was formerly known as Bro?
options: Snort
Zeek
Suricata
pfSense
questions.explanation: Zeek, formerly Bro, is an open-source network monitoring and analysis platform. Snort and Suricata are intrusion detection and prevention systems.

questions.question: How does a WAF differ from a traditional firewall?
options: A WAF filters by IP and port; a traditional firewall inspects web requests
A WAF protects email servers; a traditional firewall protects databases
A WAF filters web requests to protect web apps; a firewall mainly filters by IP and port
A WAF is installed on laptops; a traditional firewall is installed in browsers
questions.explanation: A traditional firewall filters mainly on IP, port and protocol. A WAF sits in front of a web application and filters web requests. An NGFW adds deeper application-aware inspection.

questions.question: What is the difference between ‘Block’ and ‘Reject’ as firewall actions?
options: Reject silently drops traffic; Block drops it and tells the source
Block allows traffic through; Reject drops it
There is no difference between the two actions
Block silently drops traffic; Reject drops it and tells the source
questions.explanation: Pass allows traffic. Block silently drops it. Reject drops it and informs the source that the connection was rejected.

questions.question: What does a ‘default deny’ firewall posture mean?
options: Traffic is blocked unless a rule explicitly allows it
All traffic is allowed unless a rule blocks it
Only outbound traffic is ever blocked
The firewall turns off when it fails
questions.explanation: Default deny blocks all traffic unless a rule explicitly permits it, which is safer than allowing everything by default.

questions.question: A specific block rule isn’t working because a broad allow rule sits above it. What concept explains this?
options: Default deny
Firewall rule order
Firewall aliases
Promiscuous mode
questions.hint: Rules are read top to bottom.
questions.explanation: Firewall rules are evaluated in order. A broader allow placed above a specific block can override the restriction you intended.

questions.question: What is a firewall alias?
options: A fake firewall used to trick attackers
A backup copy of the firewall’s rules
A reusable name for a host, network or port used in rules
A second firewall running in parallel
questions.explanation: An alias is a reusable placeholder for a host, network or port, so when a value changes you update it once instead of in every rule.

questions.question: What is the difference between pre-admission and post-admission NAC?
options: Post-admission checks devices before access; pre-admission limits them after
Pre-admission is for Wi-Fi only; post-admission is for wired only
They are two names for the same check
Pre-admission checks devices before access; post-admission limits what they reach after
questions.explanation: Pre-admission NAC checks compliance, like patch level or AV status, before granting access. Post-admission NAC restricts what a connected device can reach.

questions.question: What does a web proxy let an organisation do?
options: Monitor, filter and block web requests on behalf of users
Speed up email delivery between offices
Encrypt files stored on user laptops
Replace the need for a firewall entirely
questions.explanation: A web proxy makes web requests on the client’s behalf, which lets the organisation filter, monitor and block malicious or prohibited destinations.

questions.question: What does DLP do for email?
options: Detonates attachments in a sandbox to see what they do
Detects or restricts sensitive data leaving in emails or attachments
Checks the sending server is authorised by SPF
Adds an external sender banner to incoming emails
questions.explanation: DLP detects or restricts sensitive data leaving the organisation. Sandboxing detonates attachments; filtering blocks risky file types.

questions.question: What is the difference between a gateway and a hosted spam filter?
options: A hosted filter sits at the edge; a gateway filter runs on each desktop
A gateway filter only checks outgoing mail; hosted only incoming
A gateway filter sits at the organisation’s edge; a hosted filter runs in the cloud
They are the same thing with a different name
questions.explanation: A gateway filter sits at the organisation boundary or mail gateway. A hosted filter is a cloud service. A desktop filter runs on each user’s device.

questions.question: What is the difference between security awareness training and a phishing simulation?
options: A simulation teaches the behaviour; training tests it and measures results
Training is only for IT staff; simulations are only for managers
They are the same activity under different names
Training teaches the behaviour; a simulation tests it and measures the results
questions.explanation: Training teaches expected behaviour. Phishing simulations test it, producing measurable results and highlighting who needs more support.

questions.question: Warning signs, fencing and visible guards are which type of physical control?
options: Deterrent
Access control
Monitoring
Recovery
questions.explanation: Deterrents discourage intrusion before it happens. Access controls restrict entry, and monitoring controls like CCTV observe and detect activity.

questions.question: What is a mantrap?
options: A hidden camera placed near the server room door
A two-door entry area that checks identity before letting someone through
A fake login page used to catch attackers
An alarm that sounds if a window is opened
questions.hint: Two doors, one at a time.
questions.explanation: A mantrap is a two-door controlled entry area that allows identity and authorisation checks before access to a protected zone, helping stop tailgating.

questions.question: What does an acceptable use policy (AUP) define?
options: How quickly incidents must be reported to a regulator
Which firewall rules are allowed on the network
What staff may and may not do on company systems, and the consequences
How long logs must be kept before deletion
questions.explanation: An AUP defines permitted and prohibited use of organisational systems, networks and devices, including consequences for breaking the rules.

questions.question: What is a security champion?
options: The most senior person in the security team
A staff member who wins the phishing simulation
An outside consultant who tests the firewall
A non-security employee who promotes good security habits in their team
questions.explanation: A security champion is a non-security employee who promotes secure behaviour, spots issues and acts as a positive security contact in their team.

questions.question: How can a whistleblowing channel help with insider threats?
options: Staff can confidentially report worrying behaviour before it becomes an incident
It automatically blocks staff who visit risky websites
It records every phone call made inside the office
It removes access for staff who are leaving
questions.hint: A safe way to raise concerns.
questions.explanation: A confidential or anonymous reporting route lets staff raise concerns about suspicious internal behaviour, surfacing insider risk early.

questions.question: An internal workstation starts scanning other internal hosts. Which traffic direction is this?
options: Remote to local (R2L)
Local to local (L2L)
Local to remote (L2R)
Remote to remote (R2R)
questions.explanation: L2L is activity between internal systems. Unexpected internal scanning can mean a compromised host preparing for lateral movement.

questions.question: Traffic from an internal laptop to an external server is described as which direction?
options: Remote to local (R2L)
Local to local (L2L)
Local to remote (L2R)
Remote to remote (R2R)
questions.explanation: L2R is activity from an internal system to an external destination. R2L is external to internal, and L2L is internal to internal.

questions.question: What is the difference between a DoS and a DDoS attack?
options: DDoS comes from one source; DoS comes from many sources
DoS steals data; DDoS only encrypts files
They are different names for a phishing attack
DoS comes from one source; DDoS comes from many distributed sources
questions.explanation: A denial-of-service attack uses one source to disrupt a service. A distributed DoS uses many sources, increasing volume and making it harder to stop.

questions.question: An attacker tries ‘Winter2026!’ against 400 different accounts. What is this?
options: Password spraying
Brute force
Credential dumping
Pass the hash
questions.explanation: Password spraying tries a few common passwords across many accounts to avoid lockouts. Brute force tries many passwords against one or a few accounts.

questions.question: Which Windows Event ID records a failed logon?
questions.hint: One more than a successful logon.
questions.explanation: 4625 shows an account failed to log on, and its status information can help explain why. 4624 is a successful logon.

questions.question: What is a common weakness of anomaly-based detection?
options: It can only detect malware that has already been seen
It doesn’t need any baseline to work
It can produce more false positives than signature-based detection
It can’t detect any new kinds of attack
questions.explanation: Anomaly-based detection compares activity with a baseline and can catch unseen behaviour, but unusual-but-harmless activity often creates false positives.

questions.question: In Wireshark, what is the difference between a capture filter and a display filter?
options: A display filter limits what’s recorded; a capture filter limits what’s shown
Capture filters only work on saved files; display filters only work live
They do the same job with different syntax
A capture filter limits what’s recorded; a display filter limits what’s shown
questions.explanation: A capture filter controls which packets Wireshark records. A display filter shows only matching packets from traffic already captured.

questions.question: Which Wireshark feature rebuilds a whole TCP or HTTP conversation into one readable view?
options: Follow Stream
Export Objects
Protocol Hierarchy
Endpoints
questions.explanation: Follow Stream reconstructs a TCP, UDP, TLS or HTTP conversation into a single view. Export Objects extracts transferred files.

questions.question: Which Wireshark feature lets you extract a file that was downloaded over HTTP?
options: Follow Stream
Export Objects
Conversations
Hex Dump
questions.explanation: Export Objects extracts transferred content from supported protocols such as HTTP for separate analysis.

questions.question: Which Wireshark statistics view helps you spot unexpected protocols in a capture?
options: Endpoints
Conversations
Protocol Hierarchy
Packet List
questions.explanation: Protocol Hierarchy shows the distribution of protocols by packets and bytes. Conversations shows host pairs, and Endpoints summarises individual hosts.

questions.question: What does promiscuous mode let a network interface do?
options: Connect to any Wi-Fi network without a password
Block all traffic except from trusted hosts
Encrypt every packet it sends
Capture traffic it can see, even if not addressed to it
questions.hint: Seeing more than its own traffic.
questions.explanation: Promiscuous mode lets an interface capture any traffic it can see, not just frames addressed to that host.

questions.question: Why is FTP risky to see in a packet capture?
options: It’s a plaintext protocol, so usernames and passwords can be read
It always contains malware hidden in its file transfers
It can only be used by attackers, never by staff
It deletes files once they have been transferred
questions.explanation: FTP sends credentials and commands without encryption, so they can be read directly from a packet capture.

questions.question: Which command prompt command lists running processes with their IDs and memory use?
options: netstat -ab
tasklist
sc query
net user
questions.explanation: tasklist lists running processes for quick triage. netstat -ab shows connections, sc query shows services and net user shows accounts.

questions.question: Which command shows active network connections and the programs that own them?
options: tasklist
net localgroup
netstat -ab
ipconfig /all
questions.explanation: netstat -ab lists active and listening connections along with the executables behind them, when run with admin rights.

questions.question: Which command lists the members of the local Administrators group?
options: net user Administrators
sc query Administrators
tasklist /admin
net localgroup Administrators
questions.explanation: net localgroup lists local groups or the members of a specified group, useful for spotting accounts an attacker has added to Administrators.

questions.question: Which PowerShell cmdlet would you use to look for persistence set up through scheduled tasks?
options: Get-ScheduledTask
Get-LocalUser
Get-NetIPAddress
Out-GridView
questions.explanation: Get-ScheduledTask lists scheduled tasks and their properties. Scheduled tasks are commonly abused so malware runs at logon or on a timer.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of PowerShell over CMD for incident triage?
options: It runs on any operating system without needing to be installed
It returns rich objects that can be filtered and piped for deeper inspection
It can’t be abused by attackers, unlike CMD
It doesn’t need any admin rights to see everything
questions.explanation: CMD gives fast traditional commands. PowerShell returns rich objects and supports advanced filtering, pipelines and automation.

questions.question: What does DeepBlueCLI do?
options: Captures network traffic into a PCAP file
Creates forensic images of hard drives
Quickly triages Windows event logs for suspicious patterns
Manages incident cases and tasks
questions.explanation: DeepBlueCLI analyses local or exported Windows event logs for patterns like password spraying, new users and malicious PowerShell. Findings should be validated.

questions.question: Why is LSASS.exe a high-value target for attackers?
options: It controls the Windows firewall settings
It stores every file the user has opened
It manages the computer’s Wi-Fi connections
Its memory holds credentials and hashes that can be dumped
questions.explanation: LSASS holds credentials and hashes in memory. Tools like Mimikatz dump them, which is why LSASS access matters during triage.

questions.question: What is the difference between an alert and a case?
options: An alert is a tool notification to triage; a case is the formal investigation record
A case is a tool notification; an alert is the formal investigation record
Alerts are only for physical security; cases are for cyber
They are the same thing in a case management tool
questions.explanation: An alert is a notification that needs triage. When activity warrants formal tracking, it becomes a case: a structured record with tasks, evidence and ownership.

questions.question: In case management, what is an observable?
options: A supporting file like a PCAP or memory dump attached to the case
A value like an IP, domain, URL or hash that can be searched and enriched
The analyst who is currently responsible for the case
A camera feed used to watch the security operations room
questions.explanation: An observable is a discrete value linked to a case that can be examined or enriched. An attachment is a supporting file such as an email or PCAP.

questions.question: How can case management reveal that two incidents are part of the same campaign?
options: Cases are automatically merged once they are a week old
Each case is given a random campaign number
Related cases share observables, like the same IP or hash
Cases with the same severity are always linked
questions.explanation: Related cases are linked through shared observables or other common details, helping identify repeated activity, campaigns or trends.

questions.question: What is TheHive?
options: A threat-intelligence sharing platform for indicators
A network monitoring tool formerly called Bro
A tool for creating forensic disk images
An open-source platform for managing incident-response cases and tasks
questions.explanation: TheHive is an open-source SIRP for cases, tasks, observables, alerts and collaboration. MISP is a threat-intel sharing platform that can enrich its observables.

questions.question: What is the difference between a case template and a task template?
options: A case template sets up a whole investigation; a task template sets up one step
A task template sets up a whole investigation; a case template sets up one step
Case templates are for alerts; task templates are for reports
They are identical and can be used interchangeably
questions.explanation: A case template standardises the overall investigation structure. A task template standardises an individual response or investigation action.

questions.question: What is the difference between case severity and case impact?
options: Impact is how urgent it is; severity is the effect it had on the business
Severity is how serious or urgent it is; impact is the effect it had on the business
Severity is set by the attacker; impact is set by the SIEM
They both just record the date the case was opened
questions.explanation: Severity expresses how serious or urgent a case is, helping prioritise. Impact records how the incident actually affected the organisation.

questions.question: How does case management differ from a SIEM?
options: Case management collects logs; a SIEM records the human investigation
A SIEM is only for small companies; case management is for large ones
A SIEM detects suspicious activity; case management records the human investigation
They do exactly the same job in a SOC
questions.explanation: A SIEM aggregates and analyses telemetry to detect activity. Case management records, coordinates and documents the investigation and response.

questions.question: Blocking a malicious domain at the DNS server and adding a firewall block at the boundary is which containment layer?
options: Endpoint containment
Network containment
Physical containment
Perimeter containment
questions.explanation: Perimeter containment controls traffic at the boundary with firewall blocks, IPS filters, WAF policies and DNS blocking. Network containment restricts internal paths.

questions.question: Using EDR to isolate one infected laptop from the network is which containment layer?
options: Endpoint containment
Perimeter containment
Network containment
Cloud containment
questions.explanation: Endpoint containment restricts the affected host itself, such as EDR isolation, disconnecting it or applying local firewall rules.

questions.question: Moving a compromised device into a restricted VLAN is which containment layer?
options: Endpoint containment
Network containment
Perimeter containment
Application containment
questions.explanation: Network containment restricts movement within the environment through VLAN or segment isolation, port blocking and access control lists.

questions.question: After isolating a host, the team keeps watching for traffic it should no longer be able to send. What is this?
options: Recovery validation
Threat hunting
Containment verification
Lessons learned
questions.explanation: Containment verification confirms the asset can no longer perform the blocked activity. Unexpected traffic should be escalated immediately.

questions.question: What does null-routing a malicious domain in DNS achieve?
options: The domain is permanently taken down on the internet
The attacker is told they have been detected
Every email from the domain is deleted
Internal hosts can no longer resolve it to its real address
questions.explanation: Null-routing stops a domain resolving to its real destination, so internal hosts can’t make normal connections to it.

questions.question: Why should a memory dump usually be taken before a compromised machine is powered off?
options: RAM is volatile, so running processes and keys vanish when power is lost
The hard drive is wiped automatically when the machine shuts down
A memory dump can only be taken while Wi-Fi is turned on
Windows deletes all its event logs during shutdown
questions.explanation: RAM holds running processes, network artefacts and credentials that disappear when power is lost, so volatile evidence is collected early.

questions.question: What does a hardware write blocker do?
options: Encrypts the evidence so only the court can read it
Stops any data being written to the original drive during acquisition
Speeds up copying data from the suspect drive
Deletes malware from the drive before it is copied
questions.explanation: A write blocker sits between the suspect storage and the forensic workstation so the original media can’t be modified during acquisition.

questions.question: How do investigators show a forensic copy is identical to the original drive?
options: By checking both drives are the same make and size
By opening a few files on each and comparing them
By comparing cryptographic hashes of the source and the copy
By checking the copy was made on the same day
questions.explanation: Hash verification compares hashes of the source and the forensic copy to show the acquired data hasn’t changed.

questions.question: What is a bit-by-bit copy?
options: A copy of only the files the user can see in their folders
A compressed backup made by Windows each night
A copy of a single file split into smaller pieces
A sector-level copy reproducing all readable data, not just visible files
questions.explanation: A bit-by-bit copy reproduces all readable data from the source at sector level, including deleted and unallocated areas, not just visible files.

questions.question: Which tool is used to rapidly collect targeted forensic artefacts, including from live systems?
options: KAPE
Wireshark
TheHive
pfSense
questions.explanation: KAPE rapidly collects targeted forensic artefacts, including volatile evidence from live systems. FTK Imager creates forensic disk images.

questions.question: Why is reimaging often preferred over manually removing malware after a deep compromise?
options: Reimaging keeps every file the user created since the infection
Rebuilding from a trusted image is less likely to miss hidden persistence
Manual removal is not allowed under GDPR
Reimaging is faster than restarting the computer
questions.explanation: Reimaging rebuilds from a trusted pre-infection source, which is more reliable for deep compromise, though newer data may be lost. Manual removal risks missing persistence.

questions.question: Malware adds an entry to a registry Run key. Why must eradication remove that entry too?
options: Registry entries slow down the computer’s start-up
It stores the attacker’s IP address for the SIEM
It’s persistence: the malware would run again at the next logon
Windows can’t update while the entry exists
questions.explanation: Registry persistence makes malicious code run automatically. Eradication must remove the persistence entry as well as its payload.

questions.question: On Linux, which scheduled mechanism can attackers abuse for persistence?
options: A GPO
A registry Run key
A SPAN port
A cron job
questions.explanation: Cron jobs schedule commands on Linux and Unix systems and can be abused for persistence, so they should be reviewed during eradication.

questions.question: What is the difference between containment verification and recovery validation?
options: One checks the harmful activity is blocked; the other checks restored systems are clean
One checks restored systems are clean; the other checks harmful activity is blocked
Both just check that backups were taken correctly
Neither is needed if the system was reimaged
questions.hint: Two different checks at two stages.
questions.explanation: Containment verification checks that harmful activity is actually blocked. Recovery validation checks remediated systems are clean, patched and safe for production.

questions.question: After an incident, the team searches the rest of the network for the same indicators. What is this?
options: A tabletop exercise
A threat exposure check
Recovery validation
A risk transfer
questions.explanation: A threat exposure check searches the wider environment for indicators or behaviours from the incident to find other affected systems.

questions.question: What is the difference between eradication and hardening?
options: Hardening removes the current threat; eradication makes a repeat less likely
Eradication is about people; hardening is about buildings
Eradication removes the current threat; hardening makes a repeat attack less likely
They both mean restoring data from a backup
questions.explanation: Eradication removes the current threat and attacker changes. Hardening reduces attack surface so the same or a similar attack is less likely to succeed.

questions.question: What does MTTD measure?
options: The average time taken to fully restore affected systems
The average cost of each security incident
The average number of alerts raised per day
The average time taken to notice an incident has happened
questions.explanation: MTTD is how quickly the team notices an incident. MTTR measures how quickly they respond or resolve it, and remediation time is how long full recovery takes.

questions.question: What is the difference between MTTR and remediation time?
options: MTTR is how fast the team responds; remediation time is until systems are fully back
Remediation time is how fast the team responds; MTTR is until systems are back
MTTR measures cost; remediation time measures alert volume
They measure exactly the same thing
questions.explanation: MTTR measures how quickly the team takes effective action and resolves the issue. Remediation time covers full recovery and return to production.

questions.question: What is the difference between an SLA and an SLO?
options: An SLO is the overall agreement; an SLA is a specific target in it
An SLA is the overall agreement; an SLO is a specific measurable target in it
An SLA is internal only; an SLO is shared with customers
They are two names for the same document
questions.explanation: A Service Level Agreement sets broad expectations with a customer. A Service Level Objective is a specific measurable goal inside it, such as uptime.

questions.question: What does the ‘alerts created per incident’ metric help a team find?
options: How much the incident cost the business
How many staff were affected by the incident
Where detections fired or were missing along the attack path
How long the incident took to recover from
questions.explanation: Counting alerts during an incident shows where detection existed and where it was missing across the attacker’s path.

questions.question: Which section of an incident report gives a short, non-technical overview focused on business impact?
options: The incident investigation
The appendix
The incident timeline
The executive summary
questions.explanation: The executive summary is a concise business view. The investigation is the detailed technical narrative, and the appendix holds bulky supporting material.

questions.question: An incident spans offices in London, New York and Tokyo. Which timezone should the report timeline use?
options: UTC, so everything is on one reference time
The local time of each office for each event
Whichever timezone the analyst is in
The timezone of the attacker’s IP address
questions.explanation: Incident timelines are normalised to one timezone, commonly UTC, so events from different locations can be compared accurately.

questions.question: What is the key rule for evidence-backed incident reporting?
options: Keep the report vague so it can’t be challenged later
Make a point, then back it up with evidence like logs or screenshots
Only include findings the attacker has admitted to
Put all evidence in the executive summary
questions.explanation: Reports should make a point and then provide evidence such as logs, screenshots, PCAPs or case notes, rather than unsupported speculation.

questions.question: Where should a long list of IOCs go in an incident report?
options: The executive summary
The title page
The appendix
The timeline
questions.explanation: The appendix holds large tables, figures, long IOC lists and other material referenced from the main report.

questions.question: What is MITRE ATT&CK?
options: A government agency that investigates cyber crime
A SIEM product used by large SOCs
A list of every known software vulnerability
A knowledge base of real-world attacker tactics and techniques
questions.explanation: MITRE ATT&CK is a knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques used to map attacks, assess visibility, improve detections and support hunting.

questions.question: In ATT&CK, what is the difference between a tactic and a technique?
options: A tactic is the attacker’s goal; a technique is how they achieve it
A technique is the attacker’s goal; a tactic is how they achieve it
Tactics are for Windows; techniques are for Linux
Tactics are defensive controls; techniques are attacks
questions.explanation: A tactic is the adversary’s goal, like Credential Access. A technique is the method used, like OS Credential Dumping. Sub-techniques are more specific methods.

questions.question: How many tactics does the BTL1 course list in the ATT&CK Enterprise matrix?
questions.explanation: The course covers 12 tactics: Initial Access, Execution, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, Defense Evasion, Credential Access, Discovery, Lateral Movement, Collection, Command and Control, Exfiltration and Impact.

questions.question: An attacker gathers files of interest and stages them inside the network. Which ATT&CK tactic is this?
options: Exfiltration
Discovery
Collection
Impact
questions.explanation: Collection gathers and stages data inside the environment. Exfiltration is removing it from the environment.

questions.question: What is the difference between the Persistence and Privilege Escalation tactics?
options: Privilege Escalation keeps access; Persistence gains higher permissions
Persistence steals data; Privilege Escalation deletes it
They describe the same goal
Persistence keeps access; Privilege Escalation gains higher permissions
questions.explanation: Persistence maintains access across restarts or credential changes. Privilege Escalation gains higher permissions, like admin or SYSTEM.

questions.question: An attacker clears event logs and disables antivirus. Which ATT&CK tactic is this?
options: Defense Evasion
Credential Access
Impact
Collection
questions.explanation: Defense Evasion covers avoiding, disabling or bypassing security controls and removing evidence, such as Impair Defenses (T1562) and Indicator Removal (T1070).

questions.question: An attacker enumerates domain accounts and scans for open services. Which ATT&CK tactic is this?
options: Lateral Movement
Discovery
Initial Access
Execution
questions.explanation: Discovery is learning about accounts, systems and services. Lateral Movement then uses that knowledge to move between systems.

questions.question: Which ATT&CK technique ID is Phishing?
questions.explanation: T1566 is Phishing. T1486 is Data Encrypted for Impact, T1078 is Valid Accounts and T1003 is OS Credential Dumping.

questions.question: Ransomware encrypting files maps to which ATT&CK technique?
options: Defacement (T1491)
Account Access Removal (T1531)
Scheduled Transfer (T1029)
Data Encrypted for Impact (T1486)
questions.explanation: T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact covers encrypting data to deny access, commonly associated with ransomware.

questions.question: An attacker logs in using a real employee’s stolen credentials. Which ATT&CK technique is this?
options: Valid Accounts (T1078)
Brute Force (T1110)
User Execution (T1204)
Phishing (T1566)
questions.explanation: T1078 Valid Accounts is using legitimate credentials to access systems or higher privileges, often after phishing or credential theft.

questions.question: Dumping password hashes from LSASS memory falls under which ATT&CK technique?
options: Brute Force (T1110)
OS Credential Dumping (T1003)
Account Discovery (T1087)
Screen Capture (T1113)
questions.explanation: T1003 OS Credential Dumping retrieves credentials from OS stores or process memory. LSASS Memory is one of its sub-techniques.

questions.question: An attacker uses RDP with stolen credentials to hop to another server. Which ATT&CK technique is this?
options: External Remote Services (T1133)
Internal Spearphishing (T1534)
Remote Services (T1021)
Web Service (T1102)
questions.explanation: T1021 Remote Services uses RDP, SMB, SSH, VNC or WinRM to move between systems inside the network. T1133 is internet-facing services used for initial access.

questions.question: An attacker uses a compromised internal mailbox to phish colleagues. Which ATT&CK technique is this?
options: Phishing (T1566)
Email Collection (T1114)
Valid Accounts (T1078)
Internal Spearphishing (T1534)
questions.explanation: T1534 Internal Spearphishing uses a compromised internal mailbox or channel to send convincing phishing to other users.

questions.question: Malware spread on USB sticks into an air-gapped network maps to which ATT&CK technique?
options: Replication Through Removable Media (T1091)
External Remote Services (T1133)
Non-Standard Port (T1571)
Exfiltration Over C2 Channel (T1041)
questions.explanation: T1091 Replication Through Removable Media uses devices like USB sticks to carry malware, including into air-gapped environments.

questions.question: An attacker creates an inbox rule forwarding the CFO’s emails to an outside address. Which ATT&CK tactic does this fall under?
options: Impact (Defacement, T1491)
Collection (Email Collection, T1114)
Discovery (Account Discovery, T1087)
Execution (User Execution, T1204)
questions.explanation: Email forwarding rules fall under Email Collection (T1114), part of Collection. They keep the attacker’s access to data even if other access is lost.

questions.question: C2 traffic is sent over HTTPS port 8443 instead of 443 to slip past filtering. Which technique is this?
options: Web Service (T1102)
Scheduled Transfer (T1029)
Non-Standard Port (T1571)
Valid Accounts (T1078)
questions.explanation: T1571 Non-Standard Port uses a protocol on an unexpected port to evade filtering or complicate analysis.

questions.question: Malware uses a public cloud storage service to relay its commands. Which ATT&CK technique is this?
options: Non-Standard Port (T1571)
Remote Services (T1021)
External Remote Services (T1133)
Web Service (T1102)
questions.explanation: T1102 Web Service uses legitimate external web or cloud services as a relay or storage mechanism for C2.

questions.question: What is ATT&CK Navigator used for?
options: Colouring and mapping techniques to track detection coverage and gaps
Scanning the network for vulnerable services
Converting Sigma rules into Splunk searches
Managing incident cases and their tasks
questions.explanation: ATT&CK Navigator maps and colours techniques for threat hunting, adversary emulation and assessing detection coverage.

questions.question: What is the difference between threat hunting and adversary emulation?
options: Emulation searches for hidden attackers; hunting copies an actor’s behaviour
Hunting searches for hidden attackers; emulation copies an actor’s behaviour to test defences
Hunting is done by red teams; emulation by the helpdesk
They both mean writing new SIEM rules
questions.explanation: Threat hunting proactively searches for attackers already inside. Adversary emulation reproduces a known actor’s tactics and techniques to test defenders.

questions.question: Changing a malicious file’s timestamps so it blends in with system files is called what?
options: Jitter
Beaconing
Timestomping
Defanging
questions.explanation: Timestomping changes file timestamps so it’s less obvious when a file was created or modified. It’s a Defense Evasion action.

questions.question: What is threat intelligence?
options: A list of every employee who has failed a phishing simulation
Software that blocks all malware before it reaches a device
A report on how much the security team spent last year
Information that helps understand current and future threats so defenders can reduce risk
questions.explanation: Threat intelligence is information used to understand threats targeting an organisation now or in future, so defenders can reduce risk and improve detection and response.

questions.question: What is the correct order of the threat intelligence lifecycle?
options: Planning, collection, processing, analysis, dissemination, feedback
Collection, analysis, planning, feedback, processing, dissemination
Analysis, collection, dissemination, planning, processing, feedback
Dissemination, planning, processing, collection, feedback, analysis
questions.explanation: The lifecycle runs Planning & Direction, Collection, Processing, Analysis, Dissemination and Feedback, then repeats.

questions.question: Which lifecycle stage defines the intelligence requirement, scope and stakeholders?
options: Collection
Planning & Direction
Dissemination
Feedback
questions.explanation: Planning & Direction sets the requirement, scope, goals and stakeholders so collection and analysis stay focused on useful outcomes.

questions.question: Translating a foreign-language hacking forum post so it can be analysed happens in which stage?
options: Collection
Analysis
Processing
Dissemination
questions.explanation: Processing converts collected raw data into a usable format, such as translating material or normalising data, ready for analysis.

questions.question: Which lifecycle stage is human interpretation that turns processed information into conclusions?
options: Processing
Collection
Planning & Direction
Analysis
questions.explanation: Analysis is where people interpret processed information to produce conclusions, context and actionable intelligence.

questions.question: Sending a short threat briefing to executives and IOC lists to the SOC is which lifecycle stage?
options: Dissemination
Feedback
Processing
Collection
questions.explanation: Dissemination delivers finished intelligence to the people or systems that need it, in a format and level of detail that suits each audience.

questions.question: The SOC tells the intel team their reports are too long to act on. Which lifecycle stage is this?
options: Dissemination
Feedback
Analysis
Planning & Direction
questions.hint: Input from the people using it.
questions.explanation: Feedback is input from intelligence consumers that refines priorities, collection, analysis and future outputs.

questions.question: What makes intelligence ‘actionable’?
options: It has been collected from at least three separate sources
It is written in a technical format that tools can read
It’s relevant enough to support a concrete security decision or action
It has been marked as top secret by a government
questions.explanation: Actionable intelligence is processed and analysed information relevant enough to support a specific security decision or action.

questions.question: What is a threat feed?
options: A live video stream of the security operations centre
A news website that only reports on data breaches
A tool that scans the network for open ports
A regularly updated list of threat data, like malicious IPs, domains or hashes
questions.explanation: A threat feed is a regularly updated stream of threat data, commonly malicious IPs, domains, URLs or hashes, for people or tools to use.

questions.question: What is the difference between a threat feed and a threat intelligence platform (TIP)?
options: A feed is a stream of data; a TIP aggregates, enriches and shares intel from many sources
A TIP is a single stream of data; a feed aggregates intel from many sources
A feed is always paid for; a TIP is always free
They are two names for the same thing
questions.explanation: A threat feed is a stream or list of intelligence. A TIP aggregates, normalises, stores, enriches, analyses and distributes intelligence from many feeds.

questions.question: What is an organisation’s attack surface?
options: The physical walls and doors of the company’s main office
All the reachable systems, services and weaknesses an attacker could use
The number of attacks the SOC blocked last month
The part of the network protected by the firewall
questions.explanation: The attack surface is the total set of reachable systems, services, weaknesses and other opportunities an attacker could use to gain access.

questions.question: Intelligence gathered from public websites, social media and domain records is called what?
options: HUMINT
SIGINT
OSINT
GEOINT
questions.explanation: OSINT is open-source intelligence from publicly available sources. HUMINT comes from people, SIGINT from signals and GEOINT from imagery and geography.

questions.question: Intelligence gathered by interviewing or debriefing people is called what?
options: OSINT
ELINT
COMINT
HUMINT
questions.explanation: HUMINT is human intelligence, gathered through interviews, debriefings, observation and other human interaction.

questions.question: What is the relationship between SIGINT, COMINT and ELINT?
options: SIGINT is the umbrella; COMINT covers communications and ELINT other electronic signals
COMINT is the umbrella; SIGINT covers radar and ELINT covers phone calls
ELINT is the umbrella; SIGINT and COMINT are both types of human intelligence
They are three unrelated disciplines with no overlap
questions.explanation: SIGINT is the umbrella for intercepted signals. COMINT focuses on communications between people; ELINT on non-communication emissions like radar.

questions.question: Intelligence derived from satellite imagery and maps is called what?
options: HUMINT
GEOINT
SIGINT
OSINT
questions.explanation: GEOINT is geospatial intelligence from imagery and geographic information, used to understand locations, infrastructure and events.

questions.question: A report on rising cyber threats to the energy sector, written for the board, is which type of intelligence?
options: Tactical
Operational
Strategic
Technical
questions.explanation: Strategic intelligence is mostly non-technical, aimed at executives, and focuses on trends, business risk, geopolitics, budgets and policy.

questions.question: A list of malicious IPs and file hashes for the SOC to block today is which type of intelligence?
options: Strategic
Operational
Geopolitical
Tactical
questions.explanation: Tactical intelligence is immediately useful technical intel, commonly shared as IOCs for detection, exposure checks and blocking.

questions.question: A profile of a ransomware group’s motives, campaigns and TTPs is which type of intelligence?
options: Operational
Strategic
Tactical
Geospatial
questions.hint: About the adversaries and how they work.
questions.explanation: Operational intelligence covers adversaries, their motivations, campaigns and TTPs, helping defenders understand how specific actors operate.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of an IOC?
options: A company’s security policy
A known-malicious file hash
A firewall’s model number
An employee’s job title
questions.explanation: IOCs are observable artefacts linked to malicious activity, such as IP addresses, domains, URLs, email addresses, filenames and file hashes.

questions.question: What is the difference between a CVE and a CVSS score?
options: A CVSS identifies a vulnerability; CVE rates its technical severity
A CVE is a patch; CVSS is the scanner that finds it
A CVE identifies a vulnerability; CVSS rates its generic technical severity
They are the same thing with different names
questions.explanation: A CVE is a unique identifier for a publicly disclosed vulnerability, like CVE-2019-0708. CVSS gives it a standard severity score.

questions.question: Why might a vulnerability with a lower CVSS score be patched before a higher one?
options: Lower scores always mean easier patches
CVSS scores are listed in reverse order
Higher-scored vulnerabilities fix themselves
It is being actively exploited in the wild
questions.explanation: CVSS is generic severity. A lower-scored vulnerability that is actively exploited can carry more real risk than a higher-scored one nobody is using.

questions.question: How does Tenable’s VPR differ from a CVSS score?
options: VPR changes with threat intelligence and real exploitation; CVSS is fixed and generic
VPR is fixed and generic; CVSS changes daily with exploitation activity
VPR only applies to Linux; CVSS only applies to Windows
VPR is a vulnerability ID; CVSS is a patch number
questions.explanation: The Vulnerability Priority Rating is dynamic, updating with threat intelligence and observed exploitation. CVSS describes generic technical severity.

questions.question: What is a zero-day vulnerability?
options: A vulnerability that is fixed on the same day it is reported
A flaw the vendor had no chance to fix before it was exploited or known
A flaw that can only be exploited at midnight
A vulnerability with a CVSS score of zero
questions.explanation: A zero-day is a vulnerability defenders or the vendor had no prior chance to fix before exploitation became possible or known.

questions.question: What is the NVD?
options: A vendor’s list of its own product updates
A dark-web forum where exploits are sold
NIST’s database publishing information and enrichment for CVEs
A Windows tool for checking installed patches
questions.explanation: The National Vulnerability Database, run by NIST, provides published information and enrichment for CVEs.

questions.question: What is the difference between a threat and a threat actor?
options: A threat actor is the potential for harm; a threat is who causes it
A threat is always deliberate; a threat actor is always accidental
They mean exactly the same thing
A threat is the potential for harm; a threat actor is who causes it
questions.explanation: A threat is a danger capable of exploiting a vulnerability. A threat actor or agent is the person or group creating the harmful effect.

questions.question: An employee accidentally emails a customer list to the wrong person. What kind of threat is this?
options: An unintentional threat
An intentional threat
A nation-state threat
A hacktivist threat
questions.explanation: Unintentional or accidental threats cause harm without malicious intent, such as sending data to the wrong recipient.

questions.question: An inexperienced attacker uses a pre-built tool they don’t really understand. What are they called?
options: An APT
A script kiddie
A hacktivist
A nation-state actor
questions.explanation: A script kiddie relies on pre-built tools, scripts or services rather than advanced technical knowledge.

questions.question: A group defaces a company’s website to protest its environmental record. What type of actor is this?
options: Cybercriminal
Nation-state actor
Hacktivist
Insider threat
questions.explanation: Hacktivists use cyber attacks to promote social or political beliefs. Website defacement is a classic hacktivist technique.

questions.question: What usually motivates a cybercriminal?
options: Political protest
Espionage for a state
Curiosity alone
Financial gain
questions.explanation: Cybercriminals are primarily motivated by money, through activity like ransomware, phishing, fraud and data theft.

questions.question: What makes an APT different from a conventional hacker?
options: APTs are well resourced, sophisticated and keep long-term access to chosen targets
APTs only ever attack individuals rather than organisations
APTs use only free public tools and give up quickly
APTs are always lone teenagers working from home
questions.explanation: APTs are highly capable, persistent groups, often state-backed, using significant resources and tailored methods to pursue long-term goals against specific targets.

questions.question: Stealing a rival company’s product designs for competitive advantage is called what?
options: Hacktivism
Corporate espionage
Cryptojacking
Brand impersonation
questions.explanation: Corporate espionage is stealing confidential business information for competitive, strategic or financial benefit.

questions.question: Attackers secretly use a company’s servers to generate cryptocurrency. What is this?
options: Ransomware demanding crypto payment
A banking trojan stealing wallets
Cryptocurrency mining (cryptojacking)
A DDoS attack using the servers
questions.explanation: Attackers use compromised computing resources to mine cryptocurrency for themselves, a financially motivated abuse.

questions.question: Malware designed to steal online banking logins is called what?
options: Ransomware
A worm
Adware
A banking trojan
questions.explanation: A banking trojan steals banking credentials or other information used to access and steal money from financial accounts.

questions.question: What is an air gap?
options: Physically or logically separating a system from other networks
A gap in the firewall rules that lets traffic through
The delay between an attack starting and being detected
A Wi-Fi network with no password
questions.explanation: An air gap separates a system from other networks to reduce remote attack paths, though removable media can still cross it.

questions.question: What is DDoS-as-a-Service?
options: A cloud service that protects websites from DDoS attacks
A paid ‘booter’ service that lets anyone launch DDoS attacks
A free scanner that checks for open ports
A government team that investigates DDoS attacks
questions.explanation: DDoS-as-a-Service, also called a booter or stressor, lets paying users launch DDoS attacks without running their own botnet.

questions.question: In CrowdStrike’s naming convention, what does ‘Bear’ in a group name indicate?
options: Chinese nation-state activity
North Korean nation-state activity
Russian nation-state activity
Iranian nation-state activity
questions.hint: Think of the country’s national animal.
questions.explanation: CrowdStrike uses Bear for Russia, Panda for China, Chollima for North Korea and Kitten for Iran.

questions.question: In CrowdStrike’s naming convention, what does ‘Panda’ indicate?
options: Russian nation-state activity
Iranian nation-state activity
Criminal eCrime activity
Chinese nation-state activity
questions.explanation: Panda is CrowdStrike’s label for Chinese nation-state activity.

questions.question: In CrowdStrike’s naming convention, what does ‘Chollima’ indicate?
options: North Korean nation-state activity
Chinese nation-state activity
Russian nation-state activity
Hacktivist activity
questions.explanation: Chollima, a winged horse from Korean mythology, is CrowdStrike’s label for North Korean nation-state activity.

questions.question: In CrowdStrike’s naming convention, what does ‘Kitten’ indicate?
options: North Korean nation-state activity
Iranian nation-state activity
Chinese nation-state activity
Criminal eCrime activity
questions.explanation: Kitten is CrowdStrike’s label for Iranian nation-state activity.

questions.question: A CrowdStrike group name ends in ‘Spider’. What does that suggest?
options: A hacktivist group
A Russian state group
A criminal (eCrime) group
An Iranian state group
questions.explanation: Spider is CrowdStrike’s label for criminal or eCrime adversaries. Jackal is used for activist or hacktivist groups.

questions.question: In CrowdStrike’s naming convention, what does ‘Jackal’ indicate?
options: Criminal eCrime adversaries
Russian nation-state activity
North Korean nation-state activity
Activist or hacktivist adversaries
questions.explanation: Jackal is CrowdStrike’s label for activist or hacktivist adversaries.

questions.question: In Mandiant’s naming, which prefix is used for financially motivated groups, such as FIN7?
options: FIN
APT
UNC
TA
questions.explanation: Mandiant uses FIN for financially motivated cybercrime groups, APTxx for nation-state groups and UNC for unclassified clusters.

questions.question: What does Mandiant’s ‘UNC’ label mean?
options: A group that has been confirmed as state-sponsored
An unclassified cluster still being analysed or not yet attributed
A financially motivated criminal gang, like FIN7
A group whose members have since been arrested
questions.explanation: UNC means unclassified: a temporary label for activity still under analysis or not yet confidently attributed.

questions.question: Why is attribution of an attack often uncertain?
options: Attackers always sign their malware with their real names
Every attack comes from the same country
Tools, techniques and infrastructure can be shared, copied or spoofed
Attribution is only possible for DDoS attacks
questions.explanation: Shared tooling, copied TTPs and misleading infrastructure can produce false conclusions, so attribution should be evidence-based and probabilistic.

questions.question: What is a copycat attack?
options: Two separate groups happening to attack the same target on the same day
Copying the victim’s files before encrypting them
Re-running the same attack against a victim twice
Deliberately imitating another group’s tools or techniques to mislead investigators
questions.explanation: A copycat attack imitates another actor’s tools or techniques to confuse investigators or shift attribution.

questions.question: What are the three levels of attribution, from first to last?
options: Machine, human, then ultimately responsible party
Human, machine, then country of origin
IP address, domain, then file hash
Strategic, operational, then tactical
questions.hint: From the computer to the sponsor.
questions.explanation: Machine attribution identifies the systems used, human attribution the person operating them, and ultimately responsible attribution the organisation or state behind it.

questions.question: Why is commodity malware less useful for attribution than custom tooling?
options: It never leaves any traces on the infected system
Many different actors use it, so it doesn’t point to one group
It is only ever used by nation-state groups
It always contains the author’s real name
questions.explanation: Commodity malware is widely available and used by many actors, so it gives less confident attribution than unique tooling.

questions.question: An attacker uses only built-in Windows tools like PowerShell instead of custom malware. What is this called?
options: Strategic web compromise
Typosquatting
Living off the land
Fuzzy hashing
questions.explanation: Living off the land uses legitimate OS tools for malicious activity, reducing reliance on distinctive malware and making detection and attribution harder.

questions.question: How does TOR complicate attribution?
options: It encrypts files on the victim’s computer
It deletes logs on the target server
It changes malware hashes automatically
It hides the user’s real location and traffic path
questions.explanation: TOR is an anonymity network that obscures a user’s source location and traffic path, making investigation and attribution harder.

questions.question: Attackers compromise an industry news website their targets often visit. What is this called?
options: Strategic web compromise
Website defacement
Brand impersonation
Typosquatting
questions.hint: Also known as a watering hole.
questions.explanation: A strategic web compromise targets a site the intended victims are likely to visit, so visitors can be attacked or redirected.

questions.question: What is an exploit chain?
options: A list of every exploit a vendor has patched
Linked exploits and actions where each stage enables the next
A single exploit used against many targets at once
A chain of emails used to deliver phishing
questions.explanation: An exploit chain is a sequence of linked exploits, scripts and actions where one stage enables the next until the attacker achieves compromise.

questions.question: What is an exploit kit?
options: A toolkit used by defenders to patch vulnerabilities
A list of CVEs published by NIST each month
A bundle of exploit code that automates attacks on known vulnerabilities
A training course for penetration testers
questions.explanation: An exploit kit is a collection of exploit code designed to automate or simplify exploitation of known software vulnerabilities.

questions.question: Why do attackers obfuscate their code?
options: To make the code run faster on the victim’s machine
To make the file smaller so it downloads quicker
To add a digital signature to the code
To make it hard to read and analyse, hindering detection
questions.explanation: Obfuscation makes code or data difficult to read or analyse, hindering detection and reverse engineering.

questions.question: What is a backdoor?
options: A method or program giving covert remote access to a system
The emergency exit of a server room
A backup copy of a website’s files
A firewall rule that blocks incoming traffic
questions.explanation: A backdoor is a method or malicious program that provides covert remote access to a compromised system.

questions.question: An attacker uses a compromised web server as a stepping stone to reach the internal database. What is this?
options: Beaconing
Pivoting
Defanging
Fingerprinting
questions.hint: Using one system to reach another.
questions.explanation: Pivoting uses access to one compromised system as a route to reach or attack other systems in the environment.

questions.question: What does Microsoft AppLocker do?
options: Encrypts applications so they can’t be copied
Locks the screen after a period of inactivity
Restricts which applications and scripts are allowed to run
Scans apps in the Microsoft Store for malware
questions.explanation: AppLocker is Microsoft’s application-control technology for restricting which applications or scripts can execute.

questions.question: Why are TTPs more durable for defenders to track than individual IOCs?
options: TTPs are always published by the attackers themselves
IOCs can’t be detected by any security tools
TTPs never change once a group is formed
Behaviour is much harder for attackers to change than an IP or hash
questions.explanation: IOCs like IPs and hashes are easy to swap. TTPs describe how an actor behaves, which takes far more effort to change.

questions.question: What is the difference between a threat precursor and an IOC?
options: A precursor is a warning sign before an incident; an IOC is evidence of malicious activity
An IOC is a warning sign before an incident; a precursor is evidence of compromise
A precursor is always a file hash; an IOC is always an IP
They are the same thing with different names
questions.explanation: A precursor is an observable sign that may come before an attack, like scanning. An IOC is an artefact associated with malicious activity or compromise.

questions.question: Which of these is a threat precursor?
options: Ransomware encrypting the file server
Port scanning against the company’s public servers
A confirmed data breach notice
A malware hash found on a laptop
questions.explanation: Precursors include scanning, fingerprinting, reconnaissance and dark-web chatter, giving defenders a chance to act before an incident.

questions.question: An attacker probes a server to work out exactly which web server software and version it runs. What is this?
options: Host discovery
Dumpster diving
Application fingerprinting
Living off the land
questions.explanation: Application fingerprinting identifies applications and versions running on a target so vulnerabilities and likely attack methods can be assessed.

questions.question: Someone searches a company’s bins for printed documents and old USB sticks. What is this called?
options: Shoulder surfing
Tailgating
Eavesdropping
Dumpster diving
questions.explanation: Dumpster diving searches discarded material for useful information or items like documents, notes, devices or removable media.

questions.question: What is the difference between STIX and TAXII?
options: STIX is the format for describing threat intel; TAXII is how it’s exchanged
TAXII is the format for describing threat intel; STIX is how it’s exchanged
STIX is for malware only; TAXII is for phishing only
They are two competing names for the same standard
questions.explanation: STIX is a structured language for representing threat intelligence. TAXII is the protocol and service model for exchanging it, often carrying STIX data.

questions.question: Who created the Cyber Kill Chain?
options: MITRE
Lockheed Martin
NIST
CrowdStrike
questions.explanation: The Cyber Kill Chain is a seven-stage attack model created by Lockheed Martin to help defenders detect and disrupt attacks at several stages.

questions.question: What is the correct order of the Cyber Kill Chain?
options: Delivery, reconnaissance, installation, exploitation, weaponisation, C2, actions on objectives
Weaponisation, reconnaissance, exploitation, delivery, C2, installation, actions on objectives
Reconnaissance, weaponisation, delivery, exploitation, installation, C2, actions on objectives
Reconnaissance, delivery, weaponisation, installation, exploitation, actions on objectives, C2
questions.hint: Research, build, send, exploit, install, control, act.
questions.explanation: The seven stages are Reconnaissance, Weaponisation, Delivery, Exploitation, Installation, Command and Control, and Actions on Objectives.

questions.question: An attacker combines an exploit with a malicious Word document, ready to send. Which Kill Chain stage is this?
options: Delivery
Exploitation
Reconnaissance
Weaponisation
questions.explanation: Weaponisation prepares the malicious capability, such as combining malware and an exploit into a deliverable package. Delivery is sending it.

questions.question: The attacker emails the malicious document to the target. Which Kill Chain stage is this?
options: Delivery
Weaponisation
Installation
Actions on Objectives
questions.explanation: Delivery transmits the weaponised payload to the target, for example through spear phishing.

questions.question: Malware sets up a backdoor and persistence on the victim’s machine. Which Kill Chain stage is this?
options: Exploitation
Installation
Delivery
Reconnaissance
questions.explanation: Installation puts malware, a backdoor or persistence in place to keep a foothold. Exploitation is the step before, when the weakness is abused.

questions.question: How does MITRE ATT&CK differ from the Cyber Kill Chain?
options: The Kill Chain maps detailed techniques; ATT&CK is a linear seven-stage model
ATT&CK only covers phishing; the Kill Chain covers every attack
ATT&CK maps detailed behaviours and techniques; the Kill Chain is a linear seven-stage model
They are the same framework from the same organisation
questions.hint: Detailed matrix versus a simple sequence.
questions.explanation: ATT&CK maps case-specific adversary behaviours and techniques. The Cyber Kill Chain models a more linear seven-stage attack sequence.

questions.question: What is the Unified Kill Chain?
options: A seven-stage model created by Lockheed Martin
A list of every APT group tracked by MITRE
A Windows tool for mapping attacker activity
An 18-phase model combining ideas from the Kill Chain and ATT&CK
questions.explanation: The Unified Kill Chain is an 18-phase model combining the Cyber Kill Chain and ATT&CK to cover a wider range of activity inside and outside the network.

questions.question: What does the Pyramid of Pain show?
options: How much disruption defenders cause attackers by denying each type of indicator
How painful each type of attack is for the victim’s business
The order in which attackers move through a network
How much each security tool costs to run
questions.explanation: The Pyramid of Pain shows that lower-level indicators are easy for attackers to change, while denying higher levels forces bigger changes in behaviour.

questions.question: What is the order of the Pyramid of Pain, from bottom to top?
options: TTPs, tools, artefacts, domains, IPs, hashes
Hashes, IPs, domains, network/host artefacts, tools, TTPs
IPs, hashes, tools, domains, TTPs, artefacts
Domains, hashes, IPs, TTPs, artefacts, tools
questions.hint: Trivial at the bottom, tough at the top.
questions.explanation: From bottom to top: hash values, IP addresses, domain names, network/host artefacts, tools, then TTPs at the top.

questions.question: Why does blocking a malware hash cause attackers very little pain?
options: Hashes can only be blocked on Linux systems
Attackers never reuse the same file twice anyway
Changing one byte of the file produces a completely new hash
Security tools can’t match hashes reliably
questions.explanation: Hashes are high-confidence indicators, but attackers can change them trivially by modifying the file, so blocking them causes little disruption.

questions.question: Which level of the Pyramid of Pain is hardest for attackers to change?
options: Tools
Domain names
IP addresses
TTPs
questions.explanation: TTPs sit at the top. Detecting and denying an actor’s behaviour forces them to change how they operate, causing the most disruption.

questions.question: An intel report lists IOCs for a new campaign. The analyst searches SIEM and EDR data from the past week for them. What is this?
options: A threat exposure check
A public exposure assessment
An IOC watchlist
A tabletop exercise
questions.explanation: A threat exposure check searches security data for known IOCs to determine whether the organisation has already been exposed.

questions.question: What is the difference between a threat exposure check and an IOC watchlist?
options: A watchlist is a one-off search; an exposure check keeps alerting on future matches
An exposure check is a one-off search; a watchlist keeps alerting on future matches
An exposure check is automated; a watchlist is always done by hand
They are the same activity with different names
questions.hint: “Have we seen this?” versus “tell us if we see it”.
questions.explanation: A threat exposure check is an analyst-led, point-in-time or historical search. A watchlist continuously monitors and alerts when a known indicator appears again.

questions.question: A watchlist alert fires on a known-bad IP. What should happen next?
options: The affected user is disciplined straight away
The alert is closed, as the IP is already known
An analyst investigates to confirm it and decide on action
The whole network is shut down immediately
questions.hint: A match isn’t proof on its own.
questions.explanation: A positive IOC match prompts analyst investigation. Not every observed indicator automatically proves compromise, so it needs validating with context.

questions.question: What does a public exposure assessment look at?
options: Whether known malicious IPs and hashes appear in the organisation’s internal logs
Which of the company’s vulnerabilities have the highest CVSS severity scores
How quickly the SOC responds to alerts compared with others in its sector
Information about the organisation and staff that’s publicly visible and could be abused
questions.explanation: A public exposure assessment reviews publicly available information about the organisation and its people that attackers could exploit.

questions.question: An employee posts an office photo online. What could the image’s metadata reveal?
options: The device used, date and time, and sometimes GPS location
The employee’s password and username
Every other photo stored on the phone
The company’s firewall configuration
questions.hint: Data hidden in the image file.
questions.explanation: Image metadata can reveal device details, date and time and, sometimes, GPS coordinates. Visible screens or whiteboards can also leak information.

questions.question: Someone creates a fake social media account pretending to be your company. What is this?
options: Account takeover
Brand impersonation
Credential stuffing
Website defacement
questions.explanation: Brand impersonation creates sites, accounts or apps that imitate a legitimate organisation without needing access to its real accounts.

questions.question: Why does a breach at one website put staff accounts at other services at risk?
options: All websites share the same password database
Breaches automatically spread to linked services
Password reuse means leaked credentials may work elsewhere
Leaked emails let attackers reset any password
questions.explanation: If someone reuses a password, credentials leaked from one service can compromise their accounts on others.

questions.question: What is an ISAC?
options: A government agency that fines companies after breaches
A type of firewall used in critical infrastructure
An open-source tool for capturing network traffic
A trusted, often sector-based community for sharing threat intelligence
