questions.explanation: An ISAC is a trusted community where organisations in a sector exchange security and threat intelligence, giving early warning about attacks.

questions.question: What is MISP?
options: An open-source platform for storing, correlating and sharing threat intelligence
A commercial SIEM product made by Microsoft for searching security logs
A tool for capturing and indexing network packets for later analysis
A case management platform for tracking incident-response tasks
questions.explanation: MISP is an open-source threat-intelligence platform used to collect, store, correlate, distribute and share structured indicators.

questions.question: In MISP, what is the difference between an event and an attribute?
options: An attribute is a container for a report; an event is one indicator inside it
An event is a container for a report or campaign; an attribute is one indicator inside it
Events are for IPs only; attributes are for hashes only
They are two names for the same object
questions.explanation: A MISP event groups related information about an incident, campaign or report. Attributes are the individual items inside it, like an IP, domain or hash.

questions.question: What does a MISP warning list do?
options: Lists the threat actors that are currently most active
Warns users that their MISP password is about to expire
Warns that an attribute may be common or benign, like a popular domain
Lists events that have not been shared yet
questions.explanation: Warning lists flag attributes that are likely to be common or benign, such as well-known domains, so analysts avoid false positives.

questions.question: An analyst pastes a block of text from a report into MISP, and it picks out the IPs and domains. Which feature is this?
options: Fuzzy hashing
Event graph
Sharing groups
Freetext import
questions.explanation: Freetext import parses pasted unstructured text and tries to identify and categorise values such as domains and IP addresses.

questions.question: How can MISP spot that two malware samples are similar but not identical?
options: Fuzzy hashing, such as ssdeep
Comparing their SHA-256 hashes
Checking their file names match
Looking at their file sizes
questions.explanation: Fuzzy hashing like ssdeep measures similarity between files, helping MISP correlate related artefacts that exact hashes wouldn’t link.

questions.question: What does a MISP event’s distribution setting control?
options: How often the event is updated from its source feed
How widely the event can be shared, from your organisation to the public
Which analyst is responsible for the event
How the event is shown on the event graph
questions.explanation: Distribution sets how broadly an event or attribute can be shared: organisation only, this community, connected communities or all communities.

questions.question: Why shouldn’t a SOC ingest every IOC it can find?
options: IOCs can only be loaded once a year
Most IOCs are illegal to store
Irrelevant indicators create noise and false positives
SIEMs can only hold ten IOCs at a time
questions.explanation: Collecting every IOC creates alert noise. Prioritise indicators linked to actors, sectors and technologies that are genuinely relevant.

questions.question: What is the main trade-off between OSINT and paid threat intelligence?
options: Paid intel is free but unreliable; OSINT is curated but expensive
OSINT is always more accurate than paid intelligence
Paid intelligence never needs to be checked before use
OSINT is free but needs verifying; paid intel is curated but costs money
questions.explanation: OSINT is free and widely accessible but needs verification and analyst time. Paid intelligence offers curated, deeper coverage at a cost. Both should be checked.

questions.question: What does the Traffic Light Protocol (TLP) control?
options: How widely a piece of information may be shared
What actions can be taken against an attacker
How quickly an incident must be reported
Which traffic a firewall should block
questions.explanation: TLP states how widely sensitive information may be shared. PAP is the separate protocol for what actions may be taken.

questions.question: Information marked TLP:CLEAR can be shared how widely?
options: Only within a trusted community
Publicly
Only within your organisation
Only with the named recipients
questions.explanation: TLP:CLEAR may be shared publicly, subject to normal copyright or licensing rules.

questions.question: An ISAC shares a report marked TLP:GREEN. Who can you share it with?
options: Anyone, including on social media
Only the people in the original meeting
Your trusted community, but not publicly
Nobody, not even your own team
questions.explanation: TLP:GREEN can be shared within an intended trusted community, like an ISAC, but shouldn’t be made public.

questions.question: Information is marked TLP:AMBER+STRICT. Who can it be shared with?
options: Your organisation and its clients
Any member of the trusted community
The public, after a short delay
Only within the receiving organisation
questions.explanation: TLP:AMBER+STRICT restricts sharing to the receiving organisation only. Plain TLP:AMBER can also go to clients on a need-to-know basis.

questions.question: Information shared in a meeting is marked TLP:RED. What does that mean?
options: It must stay with the people present and not be shared further
It can be shared within your whole organisation
It can be shared with your trusted community
It can be published once the meeting ends
questions.explanation: TLP:RED is restricted to the specific people who received it or were present, and mustn’t be shared further without permission.

questions.question: What is the difference between TLP and PAP?
options: PAP controls who can receive information; TLP controls what actions can be taken
TLP controls who can receive information; PAP controls what actions can be taken
TLP is for emails; PAP is for phone calls
They are the same protocol with different colours
questions.explanation: TLP restricts how far information can be shared. PAP (Permissible Action Protocol) restricts what can be done with it without exposing the investigation.

questions.question: Intelligence is marked PAP:AMBER. What may the analyst do?
options: Block the attacker’s IPs at the firewall and proxy straight away
Contact the attacker directly to try to negotiate with them
Only passive analysis, with no contact with the attacker’s infrastructure
Share the intelligence publicly so others can defend too
questions.explanation: PAP:AMBER allows only passive handling so the source isn’t alerted. PAP:GREEN permits non-intrusive defensive actions like firewall blocks.

questions.question: Under PAP:GREEN, which action is allowed?
options: Hacking back into the attacker’s servers
Publishing the IOCs on a public blog
Emailing the attacker to warn them off
Blocking known malicious traffic at the firewall or proxy
questions.explanation: PAP:GREEN permits controlled, non-intrusive defensive actions, such as blocking known malicious traffic at a firewall or proxy.

questions.question: Why might an analyst avoid visiting a suspicious domain directly while investigating it?
options: It could alert the attacker that they’re being investigated
Visiting domains is always illegal in the UK
The browser would automatically block the analyst’s account
Domains can only be checked by the police
questions.explanation: Passive analysis investigates without touching the malicious infrastructure, helping avoid revealing that defenders are looking into it.

questions.question: What is situational awareness in strategic threat intelligence?
options: A camera system watching the security operations centre
A high-level update on current threat activity so teams can prepare
A list of every device connected to the network
The analyst’s knowledge of where the fire exits are
questions.explanation: Situational awareness is a high-level update giving security teams context about relevant threat activity and campaigns, so they can prepare.

questions.question: Why should a threat-intel source be verified before its information is used?
options: Unverified sources are always run by attackers
Verification makes the information legally binding
Free or paid doesn’t guarantee it’s credible, relevant or accurate
Sources can only be used once they’re verified by NIST
questions.explanation: Source verification checks credibility, reliability and usefulness. Neither free nor paid automatically means reliable.

questions.question: A government cyber agency publishes an advisory with IOCs for a new campaign. What is this an example of?
options: A threat precursor
A copycat attack
A sharing group
A government alert
questions.explanation: A government alert is an advisory from a national cyber authority that may include threat context, vulnerabilities, IOCs and recommended actions.

questions.question: What is a Cobalt Strike Beacon?
options: A post-exploitation implant giving attackers C2 on a compromised host
A Windows feature that broadcasts the device’s location
A SIEM alert raised when beaconing is detected
A phishing simulation tool for training staff
questions.explanation: Cobalt Strike Beacon is an implant providing command-and-control and post-exploitation capabilities, often abused by real attackers.

questions.question: Why monitor dark-web marketplaces as part of threat intelligence?
options: All malware is legally sold there with licences
Stolen company data or credentials may be offered for sale there
It’s where vendors publish official security patches
Dark-web sites are the main source of CVE numbers
questions.explanation: Stolen data and credentials may be sold on hidden marketplaces, so threat-intel teams monitor them for signs of exposure.

questions.question: What is digital forensics?
options: Recovering a company’s systems as quickly as possible after an attack
Testing an organisation’s defences by simulating real attacks
Collecting, analysing and preserving digital evidence, sometimes for court
Monitoring network traffic for signs of malicious activity
questions.explanation: Digital forensics is the process of collecting, analysing and preserving digital evidence, sometimes so it can be presented in legal proceedings.

questions.question: What does DFIR combine?
options: Data filtering and intrusion reporting
Disk formatting and image recovery
Detection, filtering and IP reputation
Digital forensics and incident response
questions.explanation: DFIR combines digital forensics with incident response, investigating incidents while gathering and preserving evidence.

questions.question: In digital forensics, what is an exhibit?
options: An item formally seized or submitted for forensic examination
A slide used to present findings to a jury
A report summarising the investigation’s results
A screenshot taken during an investigation
questions.explanation: An exhibit is digital media or another item formally seized or submitted for forensic examination.

questions.question: What is the correct order of the five-stage digital forensics process?
options: Collection, identification, analysis, preservation, reporting
Identification, preservation, collection, analysis, reporting
Preservation, collection, identification, reporting, analysis
Identification, collection, reporting, preservation, analysis
questions.hint: Find it, protect it, take it, examine it, write it up.
questions.explanation: The process runs Identification, Preservation, Collection, Analysis and Reporting.

questions.question: What is the difference between the preservation and collection stages?
options: Collection protects evidence from change; preservation acquires it for examination
Preservation is for paper evidence; collection is for digital evidence
Preservation protects evidence from change; collection acquires it for examination
They are the same stage with two different names
questions.explanation: Preservation protects relevant data and documents the scene so nothing is altered or lost. Collection acquires the data, such as by imaging.

questions.question: Why must a forensic report be detailed enough for another examiner to follow?
options: So the report can be used as a training manual
Because courts only accept reports over 50 pages
So the attacker can understand what was found
So a competent examiner can reproduce the results
questions.explanation: Reporting documents methods, findings and conclusions so another competent examiner can understand and reproduce the results.

questions.question: What does ESI stand for in a forensic or legal context?
options: Electronically Stored Information
Evidence Security Index
External System Image
Encrypted Storage Interface
questions.explanation: ESI is Electronically Stored Information: anything created, stored or used electronically that may be relevant to an investigation.

questions.question: What are contemporaneous notes?
options: Notes written at the end of the investigation from memory
Notes written as actions happen, detailed enough to reproduce them
Notes taken by the suspect during their interview
Notes the attacker left behind on the device
questions.explanation: Contemporaneous notes are written immediately after actions are performed, with enough detail for someone else to reproduce what was done.

questions.question: What does a chain of custody record?
options: Every command the examiner typed during analysis
The hash of every file on the suspect drive
Who handled the evidence, when, where and why
The suspect’s movements before the incident
questions.explanation: Chain of custody is a continuous record of who possessed or handled evidence, when, where and why, demonstrating its integrity.

questions.question: What is the difference between contemporaneous notes and a chain of custody?
options: Chain of custody records what the examiner did; notes record who handled it
Notes are for police only; chain of custody is for companies only
They are two names for the same document
Notes record what the examiner did; chain of custody records who handled the evidence
questions.explanation: Contemporaneous notes record the examiner’s actions. Chain of custody records who handled the evidence and how it moved.

questions.question: How many bits are in a byte?
questions.explanation: A byte is a group of eight bits, which can represent 256 different values.

questions.question: Which number system uses the digits 0–9 and the letters A–F?
options: Octal (base 8)
Hexadecimal (base 16)
Binary (base 2)
Decimal (base 10)
questions.explanation: Hexadecimal is base 16, using 0–9 and A–F. It’s a compact way to represent binary data.

questions.question: Which number system is commonly associated with Linux file permissions, like 755?
options: Hexadecimal (base 16)
Binary (base 2)
Octal (base 8)
Base64
questions.explanation: Octal uses digits 0–7 and is commonly used to represent UNIX and Linux permissions.

questions.question: What is the key difference between encoding and encryption?
options: Encryption changes format and is reversible without a key; encoding protects confidentiality
Encoding always uses a secret key, so it is stronger than encryption for protecting data
They are two words for the same process, used by different teams in different contexts
Encoding changes format and is reversible without a key; encryption protects confidentiality
questions.explanation: Encoding changes how data is represented and can be reversed by anyone. Encryption uses cryptography to keep data confidential.

questions.question: What is the difference between ASCII and Unicode?
options: Unicode covers far more writing systems than the original ASCII set
ASCII covers more writing systems than Unicode
ASCII is for numbers only; Unicode is for letters only
Unicode is a type of encryption; ASCII is not
questions.explanation: ASCII represents characters with numeric values. Unicode is a broader standard designed to represent text from many writing systems.

questions.question: In CyberChef, what is a ‘recipe’?
options: A saved list of known malicious hashes
A chain of operations applied to input data
A template for writing forensic reports
A configuration file for imaging a drive
questions.explanation: A CyberChef recipe is a sequence of operations, such as decode then decompress, applied to input data to transform or analyse it.

questions.question: Which organisation developed CyberChef?
options: MITRE
NIST
GCHQ
Microsoft
questions.explanation: CyberChef was developed by GCHQ, the UK’s intelligence and security organisation.

questions.question: How does an HDD store data, compared with an SSD?
options: HDDs use flash memory; SSDs use spinning magnetic platters
Both use spinning platters, but SSDs spin faster
Both use flash memory, but HDDs are larger
HDDs use spinning magnetic platters; SSDs use flash memory
questions.explanation: HDDs store data magnetically on rotating platters. SSDs use flash memory with no moving parts.

questions.question: What is the difference between a sector and a cluster?
options: A sector is a physical disk unit; a cluster is a file-system unit made of sectors
A cluster is a physical disk unit; a sector is a group of clusters
A sector is for SSDs only; a cluster is for HDDs only
They are two names for the same storage unit
questions.explanation: A sector is the minimum physical storage unit, traditionally 512 bytes. A cluster is a group of sectors the file system allocates to files.

questions.question: Why can slack space be valuable to an investigator?
options: It contains a backup of every deleted file
It may still hold data from files that were stored there before
It stores the operating system’s passwords
It records every time the disk was accessed
questions.explanation: Slack space is unused space inside an allocated cluster. It can retain remnants of previously stored files, which may be recoverable evidence.

questions.question: Why can deleted files be harder to recover from an SSD than from an HDD?
options: SSDs encrypt every file automatically when it is deleted
SSDs don’t store any deleted data in the first place
TRIM and garbage collection can clear deleted data in the background
Forensic tools can’t connect to SSDs
questions.explanation: TRIM lets the OS tell the SSD which deleted data can be cleared, and garbage collection erases stale blocks, reducing the chance of recovery.

questions.question: What does wear levelling do on an SSD?
options: Encrypts data evenly across every block
Measures how much space is left on the drive
Speeds up reads by caching popular files
Spreads writes across blocks so the same cells don’t wear out
questions.explanation: Wear levelling distributes writes across SSD blocks to avoid repeatedly wearing the same physical cells.

questions.question: What is a key limitation of the FAT32 file system?
options: Individual files must be under 4 GB
It can’t be read by any version of Windows
It only supports filenames of eight characters
It can only be used on SSDs
questions.explanation: FAT32 is widely compatible but limits individual files to under 4 GB and lacks modern security features like ACLs.

questions.question: What does NTFS add compared with FAT32?
options: Support for Linux-only systems
Journaling, richer metadata and ACL-based permissions
A 4 GB limit on individual file sizes
Automatic encryption of every file
questions.explanation: NTFS is Microsoft’s journaling file system, supporting metadata, ACL-based security and improved reliability.

questions.question: What does journaling do in a file system?
options: Keeps a diary of which users logged in
Encrypts the file system’s metadata
Records changes so the system can recover after a crash
Deletes files that haven’t been used in a year
questions.explanation: Journaling records file-system changes in a journal, so recovery after a crash can use it instead of scanning the whole structure.

questions.question: What does ext4 improve on compared with ext3?
options: It was the first Linux file system to add journaling
It adds Windows ACL support
It removes the need for any journal
Larger volumes and extents that reduce fragmentation
questions.explanation: ext4 succeeds ext3, supporting larger volumes and files and using extents to improve performance and reduce fragmentation.

questions.question: What is corroborating evidence?
options: Independent evidence that supports another piece of evidence
Evidence that has been damaged or altered
Evidence collected from the suspect’s own statement
The first piece of evidence found at a scene
questions.explanation: Corroborating evidence is additional independent evidence used to verify another piece before relying on it, important because digital evidence can be manipulated.

questions.question: What does ‘forensically sound’ mean?
options: Recorded with a high-quality microphone so it can be played in court
Handled with methods that preserve integrity and can be defended or reproduced
Collected by a police officer rather than a civilian investigator
Stored on an encrypted drive so nobody else can ever open it
questions.explanation: Forensically sound evidence is acquired and handled using methods that preserve its integrity and allow the process to be defended or reproduced.

questions.question: What is tainted evidence?
options: Evidence that proves the suspect is guilty
Evidence that has been encrypted by malware
Evidence whose reliability may be undermined by poor handling
Evidence collected from a public website
questions.explanation: Tainted evidence may have been undermined by improper acquisition, alteration or handling, weakening its reliability.

questions.question: What is the difference between a software and a hardware write blocker?
options: Hardware works at OS level; software blocks writes independently of the OS
Software blockers can only be used on SSDs
Hardware blockers allow writes; software blockers don’t
Software works at OS level; hardware blocks writes independently of the OS
questions.explanation: Software write blockers operate at the OS level. Hardware blockers physically intercept write signals, independent of the OS, and are generally preferred.

questions.question: What is the order of volatility used to prioritise evidence collection?
options: Registers and cache, RAM, disk, remote logs, then archival media
Disk, RAM, archival media, registers, then remote logs
Archival media, disk, remote logs, RAM, then registers
RAM, disk, registers, archival media, then remote logs
questions.explanation: Collect from most to least volatile: registers and cache, RAM, disk, remote logging data, then physical configuration, topology and archival media.

questions.question: Which RFC gives guidance on evidence collection and the order of volatility?
options: RFC 5424
RFC 3227
RFC 5322
RFC 2616
questions.hint: Guidelines for Evidence Collection and Archiving.
questions.explanation: RFC 3227 is the IETF guidance on evidence collection and archiving, including order of volatility. RFC 5424 is Syslog.

questions.question: What is file carving?
options: Splitting a large file into smaller pieces for analysis
Removing malware from an infected file
Recovering files from raw data using their signatures, without the file system
Compressing evidence files to save storage space
questions.explanation: File carving searches raw data or disk images for file signatures, recovering deleted files even when normal file-system references are gone.

questions.question: How does a carving tool tell where a file starts and ends?
options: By reading the file’s name in the folder
By checking the date the file was created
By asking the operating system
By recognising its header and footer bytes
questions.explanation: File headers are characteristic bytes at the start of a file; footers mark the end. Carvers like Scalpel search for both.

questions.question: Which Linux tool carves files from a disk image using signatures defined in its .conf file?
options: Scalpel
ExifTool
Steghide
LiME
questions.explanation: Scalpel searches a disk image for file types configured in scalpel.conf and writes recovered files to an output directory.

questions.question: Which command-line tool extracts metadata from documents and images?
options: Scalpel
ExifTool
PECmd
RBCmd
questions.explanation: ExifTool extracts metadata such as author, timestamps, device details and GPS location from files.

questions.question: Why is memory forensics important for detecting fileless malware?
options: Fileless malware is always saved to the Recycle Bin
Memory forensics can only find malware with a file name
Fileless malware runs mainly in memory, so it may leave little on disk
Fileless malware deletes the hard drive when found
questions.hint: No file to find on disk.
questions.explanation: Fileless malware operates primarily in memory, so analysing a memory dump can reveal it when disk analysis wouldn’t.

questions.question: What is the difference between pagefile.sys and hiberfil.sys?
options: hiberfil holds memory paged out of RAM; pagefile stores RAM during hibernation
pagefile stores passwords; hiberfil stores browser history
Both are Linux files used for swap
pagefile holds memory paged out of RAM; hiberfil stores RAM during hibernation
questions.explanation: pagefile.sys stores memory pages moved out of RAM. hiberfil.sys stores memory contents during hibernation. Both can hold useful artefacts.

questions.question: What is the Linux equivalent of the Windows page file?
options: Swap space
The /etc/shadow file
The .bash_history file
The dpkg status file
questions.explanation: Linux uses swap space, a swap partition or swap file, to hold memory data when RAM is full or data isn’t currently active.

questions.question: What does ACPO Principle 1 say?
options: The investigation lead is responsible for following the principles
No action should change data that may later be relied on in court
A full audit trail must be kept so results can be reproduced
Only police officers may handle digital evidence
questions.explanation: ACPO Principle 1: no action should change data on a device that may later be relied upon as evidence in court.

questions.question: An examiner has to access original data on a live device. Which ACPO principle applies?
options: Principle 1: no action should ever change the data
Principle 3: a full audit trail must be kept
Principle 2: they must be competent and able to explain their actions
Principle 4: the lead investigator is responsible
questions.explanation: ACPO Principle 2: if original data must be accessed, the person must be competent and able to explain their actions and their impact.

questions.question: What does ACPO Principle 3 require?
options: That no action changes data relied upon in court
That the person leading the case is responsible for compliance
That evidence is destroyed after the case closes
A complete audit trail so an independent examiner can reproduce the results
questions.explanation: ACPO Principle 3: an audit trail of all processes applied to digital evidence must be created and preserved so an independent third party can reproduce the result.

questions.question: Under ACPO Principle 4, who is responsible for making sure the principles are followed?
options: The person in charge of the investigation
Every police officer at the scene
The suspect’s legal representative
The manufacturer of the forensic tools
questions.explanation: ACPO Principle 4: the person leading the investigation has overall responsibility for ensuring the principles are adhered to.

questions.question: Why is a seized mobile phone placed in a Faraday bag?
options: To protect it from static electricity damage
To block signals so it can’t be remotely wiped or contacted
To keep it charged during transport
To stop fingerprints being left on it
questions.explanation: A Faraday bag or cage blocks wireless and cellular signals, preventing remote access, communication or wiping of a seized device.

questions.question: What do antistatic evidence bags and grounding bracelets protect against?
options: Wireless signals reaching the device
Water damage during transport
Electrostatic discharge damaging the evidence
Someone opening the bag unnoticed
questions.explanation: Antistatic bags and grounding bracelets reduce the risk of electrostatic discharge (ESD) damaging sensitive electronic evidence.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a tamper-evident seal on an evidence bag?
options: It blocks wireless signals to the device
It stops static electricity damaging the device
It encrypts the evidence inside
It shows clearly if the bag has been opened
questions.explanation: A tamper-evident seal visibly shows if an evidence container has been opened, supporting the chain of custody.

questions.question: When imaging a 1 TB suspect drive, what should be true of the destination drive?
options: It should be clean and larger than the source
It should be the exact same make and model
It should already contain the examiner’s tools
It should be smaller to keep the image compressed
questions.explanation: A blank evidence drive receives the forensic copy, and its capacity should exceed that of the source media.

questions.question: Which Linux command is commonly used to make a bit-for-bit copy of a drive?
options: ls -a
dd
chown
history -c
questions.explanation: dd performs low-level bit-for-bit copying of storage media or images.

questions.question: Which of these is a Linux distribution built for digital forensics?
options: pfSense
Splunk
CAINE
TheHive
questions.explanation: CAINE is a Linux distribution designed for digital forensics work, commonly used on forensic laptops and workstations.

questions.question: Why might investigators choose live acquisition instead of powering a machine off?
options: Because live acquisition never changes anything on the system
Because powering off always destroys the hard drive
Because it’s the only method courts accept
To capture volatile data and possibly decrypted data or keys
questions.explanation: Live acquisition preserves volatile runtime evidence and, with full-disk encryption, may allow access to decrypted data or keys while the system runs.

questions.question: What is forensic triage?
options: Quickly collecting high-value artefacts to get early leads
Imaging every drive in the building before analysis
Deciding which evidence to destroy first
Ranking examiners by their experience
questions.explanation: Forensic triage quickly collects and reviews high-value artefacts, like with KAPE, to generate leads before a full acquisition is complete.

questions.question: In KAPE, what is the difference between a Target and a Module?
options: Modules define what to collect; Targets define how to process it
Targets define what to collect; Modules define how to process it
Targets are for Linux; Modules are for Windows
They are the same feature with two names
questions.explanation: KAPE Targets specify which artefacts or locations to collect. Modules run additional processing or analysis on what was collected.

questions.question: What does degaussing do?
options: Overwrites every sector of an SSD with zeros
Encrypts a hard drive before it is thrown away
Uses a strong magnetic field to make data on magnetic media unrecoverable
Repairs damaged sectors on a hard drive
questions.explanation: Degaussing neutralises magnetic data on suitable media like hard drives and tapes. It doesn’t work on flash-based SSDs.

questions.question: What is the difference between overwriting and physical destruction of a drive?
options: Physical destruction lets the drive be reused; overwriting ruins it
Overwriting only works on paper records
They both leave the data fully recoverable
Overwriting sanitises data so the drive can be reused; destruction ruins the drive
questions.explanation: Overwriting replaces contents, like with zeros, so data can’t be recovered and the media stays reusable. Shredding or crushing physically destroys the device.

questions.question: What does the DoD 5220.22-M wipe method do, as described in the course?
options: Writes zeros, then ones, then random characters, verifying each pass
Writes random characters once and then formats the drive
Uses a magnetic field to wipe the drive three times
Encrypts the drive with three different keys
questions.explanation: The course describes DoD 5220.22-M as three passes: write and verify zeros, then ones, then random characters.

questions.question: Which Windows artefact is strong evidence that a program was actually executed?
options: LNK files
Prefetch files
Cookies
The Recycle Bin
questions.explanation: Prefetch files show an executable’s name, path, run count and last run times, making them strong evidence of program execution.

questions.question: Where are Windows Prefetch files stored by default?
options: C:\Users\Public\Prefetch
C:\Program Files\Prefetch
C:\Windows\Prefetch
C:\Windows\System32\Logs
questions.explanation: Prefetch files, with the .pf extension, are stored by default in C:\Windows\Prefetch. PECmd parses them.

questions.question: What can a Windows LNK (shortcut) file reveal?
options: The user’s saved passwords
Every website the user visited
The contents of the deleted file
The linked file’s path, size and timestamps
questions.explanation: LNK files can reveal the target path, file size and created, modified and accessed timestamps, even if the target has since been deleted.

questions.question: What do Jump Lists show?
options: Recent and pinned files and apps the user interacted with
Every program that has ever been installed
Failed logon attempts on the computer
The network connections a process made
questions.explanation: Jump Lists record interaction with pinned and recent applications and files, including paths, timestamps and application IDs.

questions.question: What is the difference between browser history and browser cache?
options: Cache records sites visited; history stores copies of pages and images
History records sites visited; cache stores local copies of pages and images
History is only kept by Chrome; cache only by Edge
They store exactly the same information
questions.hint: List of visits versus stored content.
questions.explanation: Browser history records visited resources and timestamps. The cache preserves local copies of web content, letting examiners see what was viewed.

questions.question: What could browser autofill data reveal to an investigator?
options: Only the browser’s version number and update history
Every file stored on the user’s local hard drive
Names, addresses and other values typed into web forms
The user’s Windows password and their PIN code
questions.explanation: Autofill or form history stores values entered into web forms, potentially revealing names, addresses, searches and other user data.

questions.question: Windows 4624 events include a Logon Type value. What does it tell an investigator?
options: Which user account was used to sign in to the machine
How many times the password was tried before success
Which files the user opened during that logon session
How the session was created, such as interactive or network
questions.explanation: Logon Type describes how a logon occurred. The course lists 2 interactive, 3 network, 4 batch, 5 service, 7 unlock, 8 network cleartext and 9 new credentials.

questions.question: Which Windows logon type indicates a network logon, such as accessing a shared folder?
options: Type 3
Type 2
Type 5
Type 7
questions.explanation: Type 3 is a network logon. Type 2 is interactive, Type 5 is a service and Type 7 is an unlock.

questions.question: Which Windows logon type indicates someone logging on at the keyboard?
options: Type 3 (network)
Type 2 (interactive)
Type 4 (batch)
Type 9 (new credentials)
questions.explanation: Type 2 is an interactive logon at the console. Type 3 is network, Type 4 is batch, such as a scheduled task, and Type 9 is new credentials.

questions.question: A 4625 event has status code 0xC000006A. What does it mean?
options: The user account doesn’t exist
The account is disabled
The password was wrong
The account is locked out
questions.explanation: 0xC000006A is a bad password. 0xC0000064 is user not found, 0xC0000072 is a disabled account and 0xC0000234 is a locked account.

questions.question: Lots of 4625 events show status 0xC0000064 for many different usernames. What does that suggest?
options: A user keeps mistyping their password
Accounts are being locked out
Disabled accounts are being used
Someone is trying usernames that don’t exist
questions.explanation: 0xC0000064 means the user doesn’t exist, so many of these across different names suggests someone guessing usernames.

questions.question: Where are the Windows Event Log files stored?
options: C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs
C:\Windows\Prefetch\Logs
C:\$Recycle.Bin\Logs
C:\Users\Public\winevt
questions.explanation: Windows Event Log files, including the Security log, are stored under C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs.

questions.question: In the Windows Recycle Bin, what is the difference between a $R file and a $I file?
options: $I holds the deleted file’s contents; $R holds its original name, path and deletion time
$R holds the deleted file’s contents; $I holds its original name, path and deletion time
$R is for documents; $I is for images
They are identical copies kept for backup
questions.hint: R for real content, I for information.
questions.explanation: $R files contain the actual deleted content. $I files hold metadata like original filename, path, size and deletion timestamp.

questions.question: Recycle Bin subfolders are named with long strings like S-1-5-21-…. What are these?
options: SHA-256 hashes of each deleted file, used to check their integrity
Serial numbers of the hard drive that the files were deleted from
Security identifiers (SIDs) linking deleted items to user accounts
Timestamps recording the date and time the bin was last emptied
questions.explanation: Recycle Bin subdirectories are named by account SID, associating deleted items with specific users. WMIC can map names to SIDs.

questions.question: Which Eric Zimmerman tool parses Recycle Bin $I files?
options: PECmd
JumpList Explorer
Windows File Analyzer
RBCmd
questions.explanation: RBCmd parses $I Recycle Bin metadata files individually or in bulk. PECmd parses Prefetch files.

questions.question: When correlating timestamps into a timeline, what should an investigator be careful about?
options: Clearly separating what the evidence shows from what they infer
Only using timestamps from one artefact type
Removing any timestamps that don’t fit the theory
Converting every time into the suspect’s local timezone
questions.explanation: Artefacts and timestamps are evidence. Conclusions drawn from timing and context are inferences and should be stated with appropriate confidence.

questions.question: What is the difference between /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow on Linux?
options: shadow holds account details; passwd holds protected password hashes
passwd holds account details; shadow holds protected password hashes
passwd is for root only; shadow is for normal users
They are backup copies of each other
questions.explanation: /etc/passwd stores account attributes like username, UID, GID, home directory and shell. /etc/shadow stores password hashes and needs root access.

questions.question: Which Linux file lists the software packages currently installed on a Debian-based system?
options: /var/log/dpkg.log
/var/log/auth.log
/var/lib/dpkg/status
/etc/shadow
questions.explanation: /var/lib/dpkg/status lists installed packages. /var/log/dpkg.log records installation and removal activity over time.

questions.question: Which Linux log would you check for user login and authentication activity on Ubuntu?
options: /var/log/dpkg.log
/var/lib/dpkg/status
/var/log/cron
/var/log/auth.log
questions.explanation: /var/log/auth.log records authentication activity such as logins. Some distributions use /var/log/secure instead.

questions.question: Which Linux log is a binary record of failed login attempts?
options: /var/log/btmp
/var/log/auth.log
/var/log/dpkg.log
/var/log/cron
questions.explanation: /var/log/btmp is a binary log of failed login attempts. faillog also records failed logins on systems that use it.

questions.question: Why is /var/log/cron worth checking during an investigation?
options: It lists every file the user deleted
Cron jobs can be abused for persistence
It stores the system’s password hashes
It records every website visited
questions.explanation: /var/log/cron records cron daemon activity and scheduled jobs, which attackers can abuse to keep persistence.

questions.question: What can an Apache access log show?
options: The web server’s administrator password
Every file stored on the web server
Client IP, timestamp, request, response code and bytes returned
The private keys for the site’s certificate
questions.explanation: Apache access logs record requests, commonly including client IP, user, timestamp, method and resource, response code and bytes, helping spot scanning or exploitation.

questions.question: A suspect ran ‘history -c’ before logging off. Why might their commands still be recoverable?
options: history -c only works for the root account
Linux keeps a hidden copy of every command forever
history -c only clears commands from the last minute
Earlier commands may already have been written to .bash_history
questions.hint: The file versus the active list.
questions.explanation: history -c clears the current shell’s list, but commands already written to the .bash_history file may remain.

questions.question: On Linux, how do you list hidden files whose names start with a dot?
options: ls -a
ls -h
dd -a
chown -a
questions.explanation: ls normally hides dot-prefixed files. ls -a includes hidden files and directories.

questions.question: What is steganography?
options: Encrypting data so only the recipient can read it
Hiding data inside other innocent-looking data, like an image
Encoding data into Base64 for email
Compressing files to make them smaller
questions.hint: Hiding that data exists at all.
questions.explanation: Steganography conceals information inside other data, such as a file inside an image. Encoding changes representation but doesn’t hide that data exists.

questions.question: In steganography, what is the cover file?
options: The file containing the password to extract the data
The report describing what was hidden
The innocent-looking file that holds the hidden data
A backup of the original hidden data
questions.explanation: The cover file is the apparently legitimate file, such as a photo, used to contain hidden data.

questions.question: What does StegCracker do?
options: Hides files inside images using a password
Extracts metadata from photos and documents
Carves deleted files from disk images
Brute-forces Steghide passphrases to recover hidden data
questions.explanation: StegCracker brute-forces Steghide passphrases so investigators can try to recover password-protected hidden data. Steghide does the hiding.

questions.question: What are counter-forensics techniques?
options: Methods that make forensic discovery or analysis harder
Methods investigators use to count pieces of evidence
Tools that speed up forensic imaging
Checks that confirm a forensic report is accurate
questions.explanation: Counter-forensics aims to frustrate forensic discovery or analysis, for example by hiding data with steganography or wiping logs.

questions.question: Which tool captures memory from a Linux system?
options: Scalpel
LiME
RBCmd
PECmd
questions.explanation: LiME (Linux Memory Extractor) captures Linux system memory for later analysis. memdump is another option.

questions.question: What is Volatility?
options: A tool for imaging hard drives bit by bit
A Linux log analysis and search tool
An open-source framework for analysing memory dumps
A file-carving utility for disk images
questions.explanation: Volatility is an open-source memory-forensics framework that uses plugins to examine processes, network activity, files and more from memory dumps.

questions.question: In Volatility 2, what is the job of the imageinfo plugin?
options: To list every process running at the time
To show the network connections in memory
To dump the files referenced in memory
To suggest the right profile for the memory image
questions.explanation: imageinfo analyses a memory image and suggests the most suitable Volatility 2 profile, which is then passed with --profile in later commands.

questions.question: How does Volatility 3 differ from Volatility 2?
options: It drops profiles and uses symbol tables with OS-specific plugins
It requires a profile to be chosen with imageinfo first
It can only analyse Linux memory images
It analyses disk images instead of memory
questions.explanation: Volatility 3 removes the need for profiles, using symbol tables and OS-namespaced plugins like windows.pslist or linux.pstree.

questions.question: Which Volatility plugin shows processes as a parent–child tree?
options: pslist
pstree
psscan
netscan
questions.explanation: pstree displays processes by parent and child, helping spot odd relationships like Word spawning cmd.exe.

questions.question: Why compare psscan output with pslist in Volatility?
options: pslist shows network connections that psscan doesn’t
psscan is faster but only shows system processes
psscan can reveal hidden or terminated processes that pslist misses
They always show the same results, so it confirms accuracy
questions.explanation: pslist shows the normal process list. psscan scans memory for process objects, including hidden or terminated ones, so differences are suspicious.

questions.question: Which Volatility plugin compares several process-listing methods to find hidden processes?
options: pstree
cmdline
timeliner
psxview
questions.explanation: psxview compares multiple process-enumeration methods to help identify processes hidden from normal listings.

questions.question: Which Volatility plugin finds network connections in a memory image?
options: netscan
filescan
dumpfiles
iehistory
questions.explanation: netscan identifies active and closed network connections in memory, including addresses and the associated process where available.

questions.question: Which Volatility plugin shows the arguments a process was started with?
options: pslist
cmdline
netscan
procdump
questions.explanation: cmdline retrieves a process’s command-line arguments, revealing how an executable was launched and what parameters it received.

questions.question: What is the difference between procdump and dumpfiles in Volatility?
options: dumpfiles extracts a process by PID; procdump extracts files referenced in memory
procdump lists processes; dumpfiles lists network connections
procdump extracts a process’s executable by PID; dumpfiles extracts files referenced in memory
They do exactly the same thing
questions.explanation: procdump extracts a selected process’s executable, normally by PID. dumpfiles tries to extract files identified in the memory image.

questions.question: Why do Volatility plugins often target a PID rather than a process name?
options: Process names are encrypted inside memory images and can’t be read
PIDs never change, even after the computer is restarted
Volatility can’t read process names, only their numbers
Several processes can share a name, but a PID identifies one instance
questions.explanation: A process name can appear many times, but a PID uniquely identifies one process instance for targeted analysis.

questions.question: What is YARA used for in forensics?
options: Rule-based searching of files or memory for malware patterns
Capturing memory from a running Linux system
Parsing Windows Prefetch files
Building a timeline of disk activity
questions.explanation: YARA uses rules to search memory or files for malware-related strings, byte patterns and other indicators.

questions.question: What is Autopsy?
options: A tool for capturing live RAM from a running Windows machine
A forensic platform for analysing disk images with automated ingest
A network packet analyser for reviewing captured traffic
A command-line hashing tool for verifying evidence copies
questions.explanation: Autopsy is a forensic disk-analysis platform built on The Sleuth Kit, with automated ingest modules and read-only file-system browsing.

questions.question: What is the difference between Autopsy and FTK Imager?
options: FTK Imager mainly analyses disk images; Autopsy is for acquiring them
Autopsy is for memory only; FTK Imager is for network traffic only
Autopsy mainly analyses disk images; FTK Imager is mainly for acquiring and verifying them
They are the same tool from different vendors
questions.explanation: Autopsy is primarily an analysis platform. FTK Imager is heavily used for acquisition, imaging, hash verification and read-only viewing.

questions.question: What is the typical Autopsy workflow?
options: Run ingest modules, create a case, delete the data source, then report
Add a data source, write the report, then create the case
Image the drive, wipe it, then create the case
Create a case, add a data source, run ingest modules, then review results
questions.explanation: In Autopsy you create a case, add a data source like a disk image, choose ingest modules, then review, tag and export results.

questions.question: In Autopsy, what is an ingest module?
options: An automated routine that extracts or classifies artefacts from a data source
The disk image or virtual machine file being analysed in the case
A label, like ‘suspicious’, applied to a file during review
The final report that is exported at the end of the case
questions.explanation: Ingest modules automatically process a data source, such as Recent Activity, File Type Identification or EXIF Parser, to reduce manual triage.

questions.question: A file called holiday.jpg is detected as an executable. What has Autopsy found?
options: Slack space
An extension mismatch
A hash collision
An encrypted file
questions.hint: The name doesn’t match the contents.
questions.explanation: An extension mismatch is when a file’s extension disagrees with its detected signature, which can indicate disguised or suspicious content.

questions.question: Why is unallocated space valuable in disk analysis?
options: It holds the operating system’s core files
It stores every password used on the device
It may contain remnants of deleted files
It contains a log of every disk write
questions.hint: Space not assigned to active files.
questions.explanation: Unallocated space isn’t assigned to active files, so it can still contain remnants of deleted data.

questions.question: Which disk image format, associated with EnCase, is commonly imported into Autopsy?
options: PCAP
EVTX
AD1
questions.explanation: E01 is the EnCase evidence image format and can be imported into tools like Autopsy. AD1 is an AccessData/FTK container.

questions.question: Autopsy can use RegRipper. What does RegRipper analyse?
options: Windows Registry hives, for activity like USB use and recent documents
Linux log files, looking for failed login attempts and cron jobs
Network captures, looking for malicious traffic and beaconing
Memory dumps, looking for hidden or terminated processes
questions.explanation: RegRipper extracts and interprets forensic information from Windows Registry hives, such as recently accessed documents or USB usage.

questions.question: What does a partition table describe?
options: Every file stored on the disk, sorted by size and last modified date
The volumes on a disk, with their start sectors, lengths and file systems
Which users and groups are allowed to read or change each file
The order in which files were deleted and sent to the Recycle Bin
questions.explanation: A partition table describes the volumes on a disk image, including start sector, length and file-system type.
